name: Kappa Light Chains by Flow Cytometry

faqs.question: What does the Kappa Light Chains by Flow Cytometry test measure?
faqs.answer: This test measures the levels of Kappa Light Chains in your blood.

faqs.question: Why is the Kappa Light Chains by Flow Cytometry test done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose and monitor Multiple Myeloma and Lymphoproliferative Disease • To evaluate the effectiveness of treatment for these conditions • To assess disease progression and response to therapy • To aid in the differential diagnosis of other haematological disorders

faqs.question: When is the Kappa Light Chains by Flow Cytometry test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test may be recommended if you have • Symptoms suggestive of multiple myeloma or lymphoproliferative disease, such as bone pain, fatigue, recurrent infections, or unexplained weight loss. • Abnormal findings on other laboratory tests or imaging studies. • A family history or genetic risk factors for these conditions. • A previous diagnosis of multiple myeloma or lymphoproliferative disease.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Kappa Light Chains by Flow Cytometry test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate the presence of multiple myeloma or lymphoproliferative disease. however, further diagnostic tests and consultation with a healthcare provider are necessary to confirm the diagnosis and develop an appropriate treatment plan.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Kappa Light Chains by Flow Cytometry test?
faqs.answer: A small sample of your blood will be collected using a needle. The procedure is typically quick and relatively painless.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Kappa Light Chains by Flow Cytometry test?
faqs.answer: Before the test: • No fasting or special preparation is required. • Inform your doctor about any medications you are taking, as certain medications may interfere with the test results. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Kappa Light Chains by Flow Cytometry test?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside the Kappa Light Chains by Flow Cytometry test include: • Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP): This test helps identify abnormal proteins in the blood. • Immunofixation electrophoresis (IFE): This test further characterizes abnormal proteins found in the blood. • Bone marrow biopsy: This procedure involves collecting a sample of bone marrow for further examination.

faqs.question: What is the Kappa Light Chains by Flow Cytometry test also known as?
faqs.answer: Kappa Free Light Chains test, Kappa Chains test

faqs.question: What is multiple myeloma?
faqs.answer: Multiple myeloma is a type of cancer that affects plasma cells, which are a type of white blood cell. It causes these cells to multiply uncontrollably, leading to the overproduction of abnormal antibodies. This condition can result in bone pain, kidney problems, anemia, and decreased immune function.

name: Trisomy (Aneuploidy) for Chromosome 13 & 21 By FISH Amniotic Fluid

faqs.question: What does Trisomy (Aneuploidy) for Chromosome 13 & 21 By FISH Amniotic Fluid measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects aneuploidies specifically in chromosomes 13 and 21 in the amniotic fluid.

faqs.question: Why is Trisomy (Aneuploidy) for Chromosome 13 & 21 By FISH Amniotic Fluid done?
faqs.answer: This test is primarily done to detect genetic conditions like Down syndrome and Patau syndrome in the fetus during pregnancy. It helps in identifying chromosomal abnormalities early on, allowing for appropriate medical management and counselling.

faqs.question: When is Trisomy (Aneuploidy) for Chromosome 13 & 21 By FISH Amniotic Fluid recommended, and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended for pregnant women who have a higher risk of having a baby with chromosomal abnormalities due to factors like advanced maternal age or abnormal results from other prenatal screenings. It is also recommended for women with a family history of genetic disorders.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Trisomy (Aneuploidy) for Chromosome 13 & 21 By FISH Amniotic Fluid are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results indicate the presence of trisomy 13 or 21, which can lead to genetic disorders. However, abnormal results do not confirm a diagnosis and should be discussed with a doctor for further evaluation and counselling.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Trisomy (Aneuploidy) for Chromosome 13 & 21 By FISH Amniotic Fluid?
faqs.answer: During the test: • A sample of amniotic fluid will be collected using a sterile falcon centrifuge tube. • The sample will be sent to the laboratory for analysis using the FISH method.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Trisomy (Aneuploidy) for Chromosome 13 & 21 By FISH Amniotic Fluid?
faqs.answer: Before the test: • Detailed clinical history, including anomaly scan report, must be submitted with the sample. • A duly signed consent form as per PCPNDT must be provided. • Follow any specific instructions provided by your doctor regarding fasting or medication. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with Trisomy (Aneuploidy) for Chromosome 13 & 21 By FISH Amniotic Fluid?
faqs.answer: Additional tests that may be ordered alongside this test include: • First trimester screening: A combination of blood tests and ultrasound to assess the risk of chromosomal abnormalities • Level II ultrasound: A detailed ultrasound examination to detect any structural abnormalities in the foetus • Cell-free DNA testing: A blood test that screens for certain chromosomal abnormalities in high-risk pregnancies

faqs.question: What is Trisomy (Aneuploidy) for Chromosome 13 & 21 By FISH Amniotic Fluid also known as?
faqs.answer: Trisomy 13 & 21 FISH amniocentesis, Trisomy 13 & 21 FISH test

faqs.question: What is Down syndrome?
faqs.answer: Down syndrome is a genetic disorder caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21. It leads to physical and intellectual disabilities. It is the most common chromosomal abnormality detected in babies, occurring in approximately 1 in 800 births in India.

name: AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Tissue/Biopsy

faqs.question: What does the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Tissue/Biopsy test measure?
faqs.answer: This test measures the presence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Non-tuberculosis bacteria in tissue or biopsy samples.

faqs.question: Why is the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Tissue/Biopsy test done?
faqs.answer: • This test is mainly done to diagnose infections caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Non-tuberculosis bacteria. • Identifying the specific bacteria causing the infection. • Assessing the effectiveness of treatment for tuberculosis or other related infections. • Monitoring treatment progress and guiding further management.

faqs.question: When is the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Tissue/Biopsy test recommended, and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test may be recommended if you have • Symptoms suggestive of tuberculosis infection, such as cough, chest pain, fatigue, and weight loss. • A history of exposure to someone with tuberculosis. • A confirmed diagnosis of tuberculosis but need to determine the specific strain. • Suspected non-tuberculosis bacterial infection in affected tissue.

faqs.question: What if the results of the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Tissue/Biopsy test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: The test reports will indicate whether Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Non-tuberculosis bacteria are present in the tissue or biopsy sample. Abnormal results may suggest an active tuberculosis infection or other bacterial infections.

faqs.question: What to expect during the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Tissue/Biopsy test?
faqs.answer: During this test: • A sample of tissue or biopsy will be collected from the affected area. • The sample will be sent to the laboratory for processing and culture.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Tissue/Biopsy test?
faqs.answer: To prepare for this test: • Inform your doctor about any ongoing medication or treatment. • Ensure that the specific site and clinical history are mentioned on the Test Requisition Form (TRF). • Follow any other instructions provided by your doctor or laboratory regarding fasting, medication, or sample collection. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Tissue/Biopsy test?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Tissue/Biopsy test include: • Acid-Fast Bacilli (AFB) Stain: This test helps screen for tuberculosis and related infections. • GeneXpert MTB/RIF Test: This molecular test detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis and resistance to rifampicin, an important anti-tuberculosis drug. • Chest X-ray: Imaging of the chest to evaluate lung involvement in tuberculosis or related infections.

faqs.question: What is the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Tissue/Biopsy test also known as?
faqs.answer: AFB Culture, Mycobacterial Culture, Tuberculosis Culture

faqs.question: What is tuberculosis?
faqs.answer: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacteria. It primarily affects the lungs but can also involve other organs such as the lymph nodes, bones, and brain. TB spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes.

name: AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Kanamycin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex

faqs.question: What does AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Kanamycin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex measure?
faqs.answer: This diagnostic lab test measures the drug susceptibility of the MTb complex specifically for kanamycin, an antibiotic used in TB treatment.

faqs.question: Why is AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Kanamycin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex done?
faqs.answer: • This test helps determine if the MTb complex is resistant or sensitive to kanamycin. • To identify the most suitable drugs for treating TB caused by the MTb complex. • To guide clinicians in prescribing effective medications for patients with TB. • To monitor the development of drug resistance in TB strains. • To ensure appropriate treatment approaches for patients with drug-resistant TB.

faqs.question: When is AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Kanamycin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test may be recommended if you • Have been diagnosed with TB caused by the MTb complex. • Have not responded to initial TB treatment. • Are at high risk for drug-resistant TB due to previous treatment or exposure to resistant strains.

faqs.question: What if the results of the AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Kanamycin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may suggest resistance to the antibiotic, requiring alternative medications for effective treatment.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Kanamycin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex?
faqs.answer: Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Kanamycin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex?
faqs.answer: • GeneXpert MTB/RIF Test: This molecular test helps detect TB and assess rifampicin resistance, another commonly used TB drug. • Chest X-ray: Imaging test used to evaluate lung involvement and assess the extent of TB infection.

faqs.question: What is the AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Kanamycin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex also known as?
faqs.answer: Kanamycin Susceptibility Test for MTb Complex, Mycobacterial Growth Indicator Tube (MGIT) Kanamycin Drug Susceptibility Test

faqs.question: What is tuberculosis (TB)?
faqs.answer: Tuberculosis (TB) is a contagious bacterial infection primarily affecting the lungs. It is caused by the Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTb) complex. TB can spread through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. It is important to diagnose and treat TB promptly to prevent its spread and manage the infection effectively.

name: HB Electrophoresis Test
preparation: No special preparation is required; inform your doctor about blood transfusions in the last 3 months. Show More

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the Hb electrophoresis test?
faqs.answer: There is no specific best time for this test. You can take it at any time of the day, as results are not affected by meals or daily activities.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the Hb electrophoresis test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required for the Hb electrophoresis test. You can eat and drink normally before the test without affecting the results.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my Hb electrophoresis test results?
faqs.answer: While severe dehydration can affect blood concentration, it doesn't change your fundamental haemoglobin types. However, staying well-hydrated before any blood test is always recommended.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the Hb electrophoresis test?
faqs.answer: No special dietary preparations are needed. However, inform your doctor if you've had blood transfusions in the last 3-4 months, as this can affect results.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the Hb electrophoresis test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional cleans your arm, applies a tourniquet, inserts a sterile needle into your vein, collects blood into a tube, and applies a bandage.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: Risks are minimal and similar to any blood test: slight pain at the needle site, minor bruising, and, rarely, fainting or infection at the puncture site.

faqs.question: What level of Hb electrophoresis test is normal?
faqs.answer: Normal ranges include HbA: 94.3-98.5%, HbA2: 1.5-3.7%, and HbF: 0.0-2.0%, with no abnormal haemoglobin variants detected.

faqs.question: What is the Hb electrophoresis test also known as?
faqs.answer: The test is also known as the haemoglobin HB blood test, haemoglobinopathy evaluation, Hb variant analysis, sickle cell screen, thalassaemia screening, haemoglobin fractionation, or HPLC for haemoglobinopathies.

faqs.question: What does the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Pus, Abscess, and Aspirates test measure?
faqs.answer: The AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Pus, Abscess, and Aspirates test detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB Complex) or Non-Tuberculosis Bacteria (NTM or MOTT) in samples of pus, abscesses, or aspirates.

faqs.question: Why is the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Pus, Abscess, and Aspirates test done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose infections caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Non-Tuberculosis Bacteria • To determine the appropriate treatment for these infections • To monitor the effectiveness of treatment • To prevent the spread of these bacteria to others

faqs.question: When is the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Pus, Abscess, and Aspirates test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: The AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Pus, Abscess, and Aspirates test is recommended when there is a suspicion of infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Non-Tuberculosis Bacteria. It is suitable for patients presenting with symptoms such as persistent cough, fever, weight loss, night sweats, or people at higher risk due to exposure to infected individuals.

faqs.question: What if the results of the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Pus, Abscess, and Aspirates test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results of the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Pus, Abscess, and Aspirates test may indicate the presence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Non-Tuberculosis Bacteria, suggesting an ongoing infection.

faqs.question: What to expect during the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Pus, Abscess, and Aspirates test?
faqs.answer: • A 2 ml sample of pus, abscess, or aspirate will be collected in a sterile leak-proof container. • The sample will be sent to the laboratory for processing and culture.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Pus, Abscess, and Aspirates test?

faqs.question: What is the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Pus, Abscess, and Aspirates test also known as?
faqs.answer: Acid-Fast Bacilli Rapid Culture by Mycobacteria Growth Indicator Tube method

faqs.question: What is tuberculosis?
faqs.answer: Tuberculosis (TB) is a contagious bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It primarily affects the lungs but can also involve other parts of the body. TB can cause symptoms like persistent cough, fever, weight loss, night sweats, and fatigue. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent its spread and complications.

faqs.question: What does the PRA Identification Class I and Class II test measure?
faqs.answer: The PRA (panel-reactive antibody) test identifies HLA antibodies in both Class I and Class II that are present in your blood.

faqs.question: Why is the PRA Identification Class I and Class II test done?
faqs.answer: • To assess the risk of organ transplant rejection • To determine the immunological compatibility between a donor and a recipient • To monitor the effectiveness of immunosuppressive therapy and evaluate autoimmune conditions

faqs.question: When is the PRA test recommended, and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend this test if • you need an organ transplant, • you have previously received a transplant, or • you have an autoimmune disease and require immunosuppressive therapy.

faqs.question: What if the results of the PRA test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: The presence of HLA antibodies in your blood indicates a high risk of transplant rejection. Abnormal results may also indicate autoimmune diseases such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis.

faqs.question: What to expect during the PRA test?
faqs.answer: • During this test, a small amount of blood will be drawn from a vein in your arm. • The sample will then be sent to the laboratory for testing.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the PRA test?
faqs.answer: • Your doctor may advise you to avoid certain medications or supplements that can interfere with your test results. • You should also inform your doctor about any medical conditions or specific requirements you may have.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the PRA test?
faqs.answer: • Cross-matching: to determine the compatibility between a donor and a recipient. • HLA typing: to identify the HLA antigens present in your cells.

faqs.question: What is the PRA Identification Class I and Class II test also known as?
faqs.answer: Panel Reactive Antibody (PRA) Test or Pre-transplant cross-matching test

faqs.question: What is organ transplant rejection?
faqs.answer: Organ transplant rejection occurs when your immune system identifies the transplanted organ as foreign and attacks it. This can lead to complications or failure of the transplant, requiring additional medical procedures to manage or remove the transplanted organ.

preparation: A high biotin dose (>5 mg/day) should be avoided at least 8 hours before blood collection.

faqs.question: How much vitamin D is needed daily?
faqs.answer: The recommended daily amount of vitamin D for adults is typically 600 International Units (IU). However, some people may need higher doses as prescribed by a doctor based on their deficiency levels and health conditions.

faqs.question: What are the differences between vitamin D2 and vitamin D3?
faqs.answer: Vitamin D2 comes from plant sources and fortified foods, while Vitamin D3 is naturally produced in skin from sunlight and found in animal-based foods. Vitamin D3 is generally more effective at maintaining blood levels.

faqs.question: Who should get the vitamin D advanced (D2, D3 & D Total) test done?
faqs.answer: This specialised test is useful for individuals taking vitamin D2 supplements or those with complex deficiency cases. It helps doctors identify the source of vitamin D and monitor treatment effectiveness more precisely.

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the vitamin D test?
faqs.answer: There's no specific best time of day for the test. Vitamin D levels remain stable in the blood. So you can provide your sample at any convenient time throughout the day.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the vitamin D test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No fasting is required for a standard vitamin D test. However, if other tests requiring fasting are ordered alongside, follow your doctor's specific instructions for preparation.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my vitamin D test results?
faqs.answer: Severe dehydration can concentrate blood components, potentially affecting test accuracy. It's best to stay normally hydrated before any blood test to ensure reliable results.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the vitamin D test?
faqs.answer: No special dietary preparation is needed. However, inform your doctor about all medications and supplements, especially vitamin D supplements, as they directly affect test results.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the vitamin D test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional cleans your arm, inserts a small needle into a vein, and collects blood into a vial. The entire process is quick and typically takes less than five minutes.

faqs.question: What level of vitamin D test is normal?
faqs.answer: The normal levels of the vitamin D test are 30-100 ng/mL (sufficiency). Levels below 20 ng/mL indicate deficiency, 20-29 ng/mL show insufficiency, and above 100 ng/mL suggest potential toxicity.

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the Chikungunya RNA Detection by RT-PCR?
faqs.answer: The test is most useful during the early phase of illness, especially within the first week after symptoms begin. Your doctor will advise the right timing based on your fever and symptom history.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the Chikungunya RNA Detection by RT-PCR, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, overnight fasting is not required for the Chikungunya RNA Detection by RT-PCR. You can eat and drink normally unless your doctor has advised fasting for another test.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my Chikungunya RNA Detection by RT-PCR results?
faqs.answer: Mild dehydration usually does not directly affect chikungunya RNA detection. However, normal hydration is recommended before any blood test unless your doctor has restricted fluids.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the Chikungunya RNA Detection by RT-PCR?
faqs.answer: No special diet is needed. Inform your doctor about all medicines, fever medicines, painkillers, previous reports and treatment history before the test.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the Chikungunya RNA Detection by RT-PCR?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional ties a tourniquet around your arm, cleans the puncture site, uses a sterile needle to collect blood for serum testing, removes the needle and applies a bandage.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: The risks are minimal and similar to a routine blood test. You may feel slight pain, mild bruising, swelling or temporary discomfort at the needle site.

faqs.question: What does Chikungunya Virus RNA PCR Not Detected mean?
faqs.answer: It means chikungunya virus RNA was not detected in your serum sample. Your doctor will interpret this with your symptoms, timing of illness and other test results if needed.

name: AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Ethionamide Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex

faqs.question: What does AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Ethionamide Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex measure?
faqs.answer: This test measures the drug susceptibility of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTb) complex to ethionamide.

faqs.question: Why is AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Ethionamide Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex done?
faqs.answer: • This test is mainly done to assess the drug susceptibility of the MTb complex to ethionamide, which guides the selection of appropriate anti-TB drugs for effective treatment. • It helps in avoiding drug resistance, improving treatment outcomes, and reducing transmission of TB.

faqs.question: When is AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Ethionamide Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended for individuals with suspected or confirmed TB infection, especially when ethionamide therapy is being considered. It is also useful for patients who have not responded to initial anti-TB treatment or have a history of drug-resistant TB.

faqs.question: What if the results of the AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Ethionamide Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results indicate that the bacteria is resistant to ethionamide, which may point towards the need for alternative anti-TB drugs or a different treatment approach.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Ethionamide Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex?
faqs.answer: Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Ethionamide Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex?
faqs.answer: • Sputum Smear Microscopy: This test helps in the initial diagnosis of TB by examining a sputum sample under a microscope for the presence of acid-fast bacilli. • GeneXpert MTB/RIF: This molecular test detects the presence of MTb and evaluates resistance to rifampicin, another important anti-TB drug.

faqs.question: What is the AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Ethionamide Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex also known as?
faqs.answer: Antibiogram for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTb) complex, Ethionamide Drug Susceptibility Testing for TB, Ethionamide Sensitivity Testing

faqs.question: What is tuberculosis (TB)?
faqs.answer: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease caused by the bacteria Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It primarily affects the lungs but can also affect other parts of the body. TB can cause symptoms such as coughing, fever, weight loss, and fatigue. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are essential to prevent complications and stop the spread of the disease.

faqs.question: What does the Threonine Quantitative Plasma Test measure?
faqs.answer: This test measures the amount of threonine in your plasma.

faqs.question: Why is Threonine Quantitative Plasma Test done?
faqs.answer: • To identify metabolic disorders or inborn errors of metabolism that cause threonine metabolism to be altered • To monitor patients with known metabolic conditions • To assess nutritional status, as well as evaluate the effectiveness of dietary interventions

faqs.question: When is Threonine Test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend this test if • you have suspected or confirmed metabolic disorders that affect threonine metabolism, or • you suffer from symptoms such as poor appetite, developmental delays, lethargy, seizures, or unexplained failure to thrive.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Threonine Test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: • Elevated levels of threonine might be due to liver cirrhosis, hepatitis, kidney dysfunction, or certain inherited metabolic diseases. • Decreased levels of threonine may be due to an inadequate intake of protein or a problem with amino acid transport or metabolism.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Threonine Test?
faqs.answer: The technician will draw a small amount of blood from your arm, and the sample will be sent to the laboratory for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Threonine Plasma Test?
faqs.answer: • Fast for at least 8 hours before the test per your doctor's advice. • Inform your doctor if you have any medications or supplements that might interfere with the test or if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with Threonine Test?
faqs.answer: • Amino acid analysis • Urine organic acids • Nutritional status assessment • Genetic testing

faqs.question: What is the Threonine Quantitative Plasma Test also known as?
faqs.answer: Quantitative Plasma Amino Acid Analysis or Threonine Blood Test

faqs.question: What are metabolic disorders?
faqs.answer: Metabolic disorders are conditions where there is an abnormal chemical reaction in your body involving nutrients from food. When this happens, it can cause an imbalance of nutrients, leading to various medical issues.

faqs.question: What are Inborn Errors of Metabolism?
faqs.answer: Inborn errors of metabolism (IEMs) are a group of genetic disorders that affect how the body breaks down food and uses energy. These disorders are caused by defects in specific enzymes that are involved in metabolic pathways. When these enzymes are not working properly, certain substances can build up in the body, leading to a variety of symptoms. Some common IEMs include Phenylketonuria (PKU), Galactosemia, Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD), Fructose intolerance, Fatty acid oxidation defects, Lysosomal storage disorders, Mitochondrial disorders.

faqs.question: What does Threonine Quantitative Urine Test measure?
faqs.answer: The Threonine Quantitative Urine Test measures the amount of threonine in your newborn's urine sample.

faqs.question: Why is Threonine Quantitative Urine Test done?
faqs.answer: • To identify metabolic disorders that affect the threonine pathway • To detect inborn errors of metabolism • To detect vitamin B6 insufficiency

faqs.question: When is the Threonine Test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: • If your doctor suspects any metabolic disorder or inborn errors of metabolism, they may order this test. Common indications include muscle weakness, developmental delay, or liver disease. • Newborns are also tested to detect metabolic disorders that can cause serious health problems early on.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Threonine Test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Elevated levels may indicate metabolic disorders such as liver disease, multiple sclerosis, or even cancer. Low levels could indicate malnutrition or digestive issues.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Threonine Urine Test?
faqs.answer: • Provide a 10-ml spot urine sample of your newborn. • The sample will be taken to a laboratory for testing.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Threonine Test?
faqs.answer: • Follow the fasting recommendations of your doctor. • Stop amino acid supplementation or medication for some time before the test. • Inform your doctor if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Threonine Test?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside the Threonine Quantitative Urine Test include complete blood count, liver function tests, and other urine organic acid tests.

faqs.question: What is the Threonine Quantitative Urine Test also known as?
faqs.answer: Quantitative amino acid threonine analysis of urine

faqs.question: What is metabolic disorder?
faqs.answer: Metabolic disorders occur when abnormal chemical reactions in the body disrupt normal metabolic processes. These disorders can impact an individual's ability to process certain nutrients and can lead to various health issues including digestion problems, organ dysfunction, and developmental delay.

name: Ferritin Test
preparation: High biotin dose (>5 mg/day) should be avoided at least 8 hrs before blood collection.

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the ferritin test?
faqs.answer: Due to natural daily variations in ferritin levels, the best time to take the test is between 8-10 AM or 4-6 PM. However, always follow your doctor’s specific instructions, as timing may vary based on your individual health needs or medical history.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the ferritin test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: Overnight fasting is not required for the ferritin test. However, consult your doctor for specific preparation instructions based on your individual health needs.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my ferritin test results?
faqs.answer: Yes, dehydration can affect blood test results by concentrating blood components, potentially making ferritin levels appear falsely elevated. Stay well-hydrated before your test for accurate results.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the ferritin test?
faqs.answer: Avoid high biotin supplements (>5 mg/day) for at least 8 hours before testing. Inform your doctor about all medications and supplements you're taking for guidance.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the ferritin test?
faqs.answer: A trained phlebotomist cleans your arm with antiseptic, ties an elastic band around your upper arm, inserts a small needle into a vein, and collects blood in a vial. The entire process is quick and takes only a few minutes.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: The ferritin blood test carries minimal risks similar to any standard blood draw. You may experience slight pain, minor bruising, or feel dizzy. Serious complications like infection are very rare.

faqs.question: What level of ferritin test is normal?
faqs.answer: Normal ferritin levels according to the reference range are 13-150 ng/mL. However, discuss your specific results with your doctor for accurate interpretation based on your health.

faqs.question: What is the ferritin test also known as?
faqs.answer: The ferritin blood test is also commonly known as Serum Ferritin or Ferritin, Serum.

faqs.question: What does the Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) test measure?
faqs.answer: This test measures the concentration of alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) in the blood serum.

faqs.question: Why is the Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) test done?
faqs.answer: The test is typically performed to diagnose and monitor conditions related to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, a genetic disorder that can lead to lung and liver problems.

faqs.question: When is the Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) test recommended, and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended when there is suspicion of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency or related lung and liver conditions, especially in individuals with symptoms like shortness of breath, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), or liver disease.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) test are positive?
faqs.answer: A positive result may indicate abnormal alpha-1 antitrypsin levels in the blood serum, suggesting the possibility of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency or related conditions. Further diagnostic tests and medical evaluation are necessary to confirm the diagnosis and develop a treatment plan.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) test?
faqs.answer: The test involves a blood draw, where a healthcare professional collects a serum sample from a vein, typically in the arm. The procedure is minimally invasive and relatively quick.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) test?
faqs.answer: Patients typically do not need specific preparations before the test. However, it's important to follow any instructions provided by the healthcare provider.

faqs.question: Which other tests are ordered with the Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) test?
faqs.answer: Additional tests and imaging studies may be ordered to assess lung and liver function and confirm the diagnosis of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency or related conditions.

faqs.question: What is the Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) test also known as?
faqs.answer: The Alpha-1 Antitrypsin (AAT) test may also be referred to as the serum AAT test or the AAT blood test.

faqs.question: Why is the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Pus test done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose fungal infections in patients with symptoms such as persistent fever, skin rashes, or respiratory issues • To monitor the effectiveness of antifungal treatment • To guide clinicians in selecting appropriate antifungal medications • To identify rare or emerging fungal species that may require special treatment

faqs.question: When is the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Pus test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor might recommend this test if you have • Symptoms suggestive of a fungal infection, such as persistent fever, cough, skin rashes, or nail abnormalities. • A history of recurrent or chronic fungal infections. • A compromised immune system due to conditions like HIV, cancer, or organ transplantation. • Recently travelled to areas with a high prevalence of fungal infections.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Pus test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate a fungal infection that requires treatment.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Pus test?

faqs.question: What is a fungal infection?
faqs.answer: A fungal infection is a condition caused by the overgrowth of fungi in or on the body. Common types of fungal infections include athlete's foot, yeast infections, and ringworm.

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the proteins/creatinine ratio?
faqs.answer: The first-morning urine sample is considered best, as it's more concentrated after overnight rest. However, a random spot sample can be collected at any convenient time during the day.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the proteins/creatinine ratio, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required for this test. You can eat and drink normally before providing your urine sample unless your doctor gives specific instructions otherwise.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my proteins/creatinine ratio results?
faqs.answer: While the ratio corrects for urine concentration variations, severe dehydration can temporarily strain the kidneys and may slightly alter results. Maintain normal hydration when taking the test.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the proteins/creatinine ratio?
faqs.answer: No special dietary preparation needed. Avoid intense exercise for 24 hours before testing. Inform your doctor about all medications, vitamins, and supplements you're currently taking.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the proteins/creatinine ratio?
faqs.answer: This test doesn't require a blood draw. It's performed exclusively on a urine sample. You'll receive a sterile container to provide a clean-catch mid-stream urine sample.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: There are no risks associated with this test. Providing a urine sample is completely non-invasive and safe, with no potential complications or side effects.

faqs.question: What level of proteins/creatinine ratio is normal?
faqs.answer: Normal levels are less than 0.2 mg/mg. Results between 0.2 and 2.0 mg/mg indicate moderately increased protein levels, while values above 2.0 mg/mg suggest severely increased levels requiring medical evaluation.

faqs.question: What is the proteins/creatinine ratio also known as?
faqs.answer: The test is also called the Urine Albumin-to-Creatinine Ratio (UACR), Albumin/Creatinine Ratio (ACR), Urine Protein-to-Creatinine Ratio (UPCR), or Spot Urine for Proteins/Creatinine Ratio.

faqs.question: What does the Conventional Method test measure?
faqs.answer: The Conventional Method in cytopathology measures the presence of abnormal cellular morphology, particularly in cervical cytology, to screen for and diagnose pre-cancerous or cancerous conditions.

faqs.question: Why is the Conventional Method test done?
faqs.answer: This kind of test provides valuable information on blood parameters, hormone levels, organ function, and more. It is performed for several reasons, including: • Diagnosing diseases and conditions • Monitoring treatment effectiveness • Assessing organ function • Evaluating overall health status • Detecting abnormalities or imbalances in the body

faqs.question: When is the Conventional Method test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: The By Conventional Method test may be recommended in the following situations: • When there are unexplained symptoms or health concerns • To monitor chronic conditions or ongoing treatments • As part of routine check-ups to assess overall health • For pre-employment or pre-operative evaluations • Based on a doctor's discretion considering individual patient needs

faqs.question: What if the results of the Conventional Method test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: If the results of the By Conventional Method test are abnormal, it may indicate an underlying health condition or disease.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Conventional Method test?
faqs.answer: The procedure is generally simple and painless. Here's what to expect: • You may be asked to provide a sample of blood, urine, or other bodily fluids. • The sample collection process is usually quick and straightforward. • The samples will be sent to a laboratory for analysis using established techniques.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Conventional Method test?
faqs.answer: To prepare for the By Conventional Method test, follow these guidelines: • Fasting: In certain cases, fasting before the test may be necessary. Your doctor will provide specific instructions if needed. • Medications: Inform your healthcare provider about any medications you are taking as they may interfere with the test results. • Other instructions: Your doctor will provide any additional instructions based on your specific needs.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Conventional Method test?
faqs.answer: Depending on the specific health concerns, your doctor may order additional tests alongside the By Conventional Method test. These may include: • Imaging tests such as X-rays, CT scans, or MRIs to assess internal structures • Microbiological tests to identify infections or pathogens • Genetic tests to evaluate inherited conditions or assess disease risk

faqs.question: What is the Conventional Method test also known as?
faqs.answer: Pap smear or Pap test

faqs.question: What is Cervical Cancer?
faqs.answer: Cervical cancer is a type of cancer that develops in the cells of the cervix, which is the lower part of the uterus (womb) that connects to the vagina. It is primarily caused by certain strains of the human papillomavirus (HPV), a sexually transmitted infection. Cervical cancer often starts with the gradual development of precancerous changes in the cells of the cervix, which, if left untreated, can progress to invasive cancer. Common symptoms may include abnormal vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain, pain during sexual intercourse, and unusual vaginal discharge. Regular cervical cancer screening, such as Pap smears or HPV testing, is crucial for early detection and successful treatment, and vaccines are available to prevent certain HPV infections that can lead to cervical cancer. Treatment options for cervical cancer may include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or a combination thereof, depending on the stage and extent of the disease.

faqs.answer: The best time is early morning, between 7 and 10 am, when testosterone levels naturally peak. This timing ensures the most accurate representation of your body's hormone production.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the testosterone total serum test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: Overnight fasting is not mandatory for this test. However, your doctor may recommend it if other tests requiring fasting are done simultaneously.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my testosterone total serum test results?

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the testosterone total serum test?
faqs.answer: Follow your normal diet unless instructed otherwise. Inform your doctor about all medications, especially hormones, steroids, or supplements, as these can significantly affect testosterone levels.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the testosterone total serum test?
faqs.answer: A trained phlebotomist cleans your arm, locates a vein, and uses a sterile needle to collect blood into a special tube. The procedure takes just minutes.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the Homocysteine Test?
faqs.answer: No fasting is required for the Homocysteine Test. You can eat and drink as usual, but always follow your doctor’s instructions based on your specific health needs or other tests.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the Homocysteine Test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: Overnight fasting is not mandatory for the Homocysteine Test. You can eat and drink as usual. However, follow your doctor’s guidance for any specific instructions.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my Homocysteine Test results?
faqs.answer: Yes, dehydration can concentrate blood components and potentially lead to falsely elevated homocysteine readings. Stay normally hydrated for accurate results.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the Homocysteine Test?
faqs.answer: You can follow your normal diet and take your regular medications before the Homocysteine Test. However, inform your doctor about all medications, as certain medicines like methotrexate, carbamazepine, phenytoin, and anticonvulsants can increase homocysteine levels.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the Homocysteine Test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional will tie a band around your upper arm, clean the area, and insert a small needle into a vein. Blood is collected into a vial, and the procedure typically takes less than five minutes.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: The risks are minimal and similar to any standard blood test. You may experience slight pain or bruising at the needle site, feel lightheaded, or in rare cases, develop an infection.

faqs.question: What level of Homocysteine Test is normal?
faqs.answer: Normal homocysteine levels are typically 5-15 μmol/L. Levels above 15 μmol/L are considered moderately elevated and may require medical attention and treatment.

faqs.question: What is the Homocysteine Test also known as?
faqs.answer: The test is also known as Total Homocysteine or Plasma Total Homocysteine.

faqs.question: What does a positive Beta D Glucan Test mean?
faqs.answer: A positive result indicates the likely presence of an invasive fungal infection, but further tests such as cultures or imaging are needed to confirm.

faqs.question: Can antibiotics affect the Beta D Glucan Test results?
faqs.answer: Yes, certain beta-lactam antibiotics and immunoglobulin treatments can sometimes cause false-positive results.

faqs.question: Is fasting required for the Beta D Glucan Test?
faqs.answer: No fasting is needed. You can eat and drink as usual before the test.

faqs.question: Can this test identify the exact fungal species?
faqs.answer: No, the test detects the presence of fungal cell wall components but does not specify the fungal type.

faqs.question: Can dialysis affect my test result?
faqs.answer: Yes, using cellulose-based dialysis membranes may cause false-positive results due to glucan contamination.

faqs.question: How accurate is the Beta D Glucan Test?
faqs.answer: It has a high negative predictive value, meaning a negative result strongly rules out invasive fungal infection.

faqs.question: What is the normal range for Beta D Glucan?
faqs.answer: Less than 0.06 ng/mL is considered negative; 0.06–0.1 ng/mL requires follow-up, and above 0.1 ng/mL indicates high risk.

name: Aspergillosis IgG Antibodies by EIA – Serum

faqs.question: What does the Aspergillosis IgG Antibodies by EIA Serum test measure?
faqs.answer: This test evaluates the levels of Aspergillus IgG antibodies in your blood.

faqs.question: Why is the Aspergillosis IgG Antibodies by EIA Serum test done?
faqs.answer: • This test is primarily done to diagnose and monitor Aspergillosis, a fungal infection caused by the Aspergillus fungus. • It can also be used to assess the effectiveness of treatment and monitor disease progression. • Additionally, this test may be recommended to evaluate the risk of developing Aspergillosis in patients with compromised immune systems.

faqs.question: When is the Aspergillosis IgG Antibodies by EIA Serum test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend this test if you have symptoms suggestive of Aspergillosis, such as persistent cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, or fever. People this test may be recommended for include: • Individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing organ transplantation • Patients with underlying lung conditions like asthma or cystic fibrosis • Individuals with prolonged use of corticosteroids or immunosuppressant medications • Patients who have been exposed to Aspergillus in their environment, such as farmers or construction workers

faqs.question: What if the results of the Aspergillosis IgG Antibodies by EIA Serum test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Elevated levels of these antibodies may indicate an active or past Aspergillus infection. However, abnormal results do not confirm the presence of Aspergillosis. Further evaluation, including imaging tests and clinical correlation, is necessary to establish a diagnosis.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Aspergillosis IgG Antibodies by EIA Serum test?
faqs.answer: To perform this test: • A small sample of your blood will be drawn from a vein in your arm. • The procedure is quick and relatively painless. • The collected blood sample will be sent to a laboratory for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Aspergillosis IgG Antibodies by EIA Serum test?
faqs.answer: There are no specific preparations required before this test. However, it is essential to provide accurate information about any medications you are currently taking or any allergies you may have. Inform your healthcare provider about any ongoing infections or illnesses. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Aspergillosis IgG Antibodies by EIA Serum test?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside the Aspergillosis IgG Antibodies by EIA Serum test include: • Chest X-ray or CT scan: To evaluate lung involvement and identify any abnormalities caused by Aspergillosis. • Fungal culture: To directly identify the presence of Aspergillus fungus in a clinical specimen. • Blood tests: To assess overall immune function and rule out other underlying conditions.

faqs.question: What is the Aspergillosis IgG Antibodies by EIA Serum test also known as?
faqs.answer: This test may also be referred to as Aspergillus IgG antibodies test or Aspergillus serology.

faqs.question: What is aspergillosis?
faqs.answer: Aspergillosis is a fungal infection caused by the Aspergillus fungus. It primarily affects the lungs but can spread to other organs in individuals with weakened immune systems. Symptoms may vary depending on the site of infection and can range from mild respiratory symptoms to severe invasive disease. Early diagnosis and proper treatment are crucial for managing Aspergillosis effectively.

faqs.question: What are the risks associated with vitamin B12 deficiency?
faqs.answer: Untreated vitamin B12 deficiency can lead to serious complications, including megaloblastic anaemia, permanent nerve damage, memory loss, confusion, and increased cardiovascular disease risk due to elevated homocysteine levels.

faqs.question: Can vitamin B12 deficiency cause depression?
faqs.answer: Yes, there is a strong connection. Vitamin B12 is essential for producing brain chemicals that affect mood. A deficiency can contribute to or worsen symptoms of depression and anxiety disorders.

faqs.question: Name some of the vitamin B12-rich fruits.
faqs.answer: This is a common misconception. Fruits do not naturally contain significant amounts of vitamin B12. B12 is produced by microorganisms and found almost exclusively in animal products and fortified foods.

faqs.question: What are the best vitamin B12 sources for vegetarians?
faqs.answer: For vegetarians, the best sources include dairy products like milk, curd, paneer, and cheese, plus fortified foods such as breakfast cereals, nutritional yeast, and fortified plant-based milk alternatives.

faqs.question: What are some common vitamin B12 sources in non-vegetarian foods?
faqs.answer: Excellent non-vegetarian sources include fatty fish like tuna and salmon, shellfish, organ meats like liver, red meat, eggs, and poultry, which provide readily absorbable vitamin B12.

faqs.question: How can I ensure I'm getting enough vitamin B12 if I follow a vegetarian or vegan diet?
faqs.answer: The most reliable approach is regularly consuming B12-fortified foods or taking vitamin B12 supplements. Consulting a doctor or registered dietitian helps determine the right dosage and frequency.

faqs.question: What medications should not be taken with B12?
faqs.answer: Certain medications can interfere with B12 absorption, including metformin for diabetes, proton pump inhibitors for acid reflux, H2 blockers, and some antibiotics and anticonvulsants when used long-term.

faqs.question: How long does it take for B12 supplements to work?
faqs.answer: General symptoms like fatigue may improve within weeks. However, neurological symptoms may take several months to improve, and severe, long-standing deficiency may cause some permanent nerve damage.

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the vitamin B12 test?
faqs.answer: The test can be taken at any time, but laboratories often prefer morning samples for consistency with reference ranges because fasting may be recommended in some cases.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the vitamin B12 test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, overnight fasting is not required for a vit B12 test. However, consult your doctor and follow their instructions, as individual cases may vary based on medical history.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my vitamin B12 test results?
faqs.answer: Yes, dehydration reduces blood fluid volume, making it more concentrated. This can falsely increase measured vitamin B12 levels, potentially masking a deficiency. Stay well-hydrated before your test.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the vitamin B12 test?
faqs.answer: You can eat and drink normally before a vitamin B12 test. Inform your doctor about all medications and supplements, especially biotin, which can interfere with results if taken recently.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the vitamin B12 test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional ties a tourniquet around your upper arm, cleans the area with an antiseptic, and then inserts a small needle into the vein to collect blood. The quick procedure takes less than five minutes.

faqs.question: What level of vitamin B12 is normal?
faqs.answer: Based on the reference range, normal B12 levels are 197-771 pg/mL. Values below this range may indicate deficiency, while levels above may suggest excessive supplementation or other conditions.

faqs.question: What does the DSA Test measure?
faqs.answer: The DSA Test measures HLA antigens on blood cells to assess compatibility for organ transplantation.

faqs.question: Why is the DSA Test done?
faqs.answer: • To assess compatibility between organ transplant donors and recipients • To determine the risk of organ rejection after transplantation • To monitor the effectiveness of immunosuppressive therapy post-transplantation • To identify antibodies that may cause complications during pregnancy or blood transfusions

faqs.question: When is DSA Test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: The DSA Test is recommended for individuals who • are scheduled to undergo organ transplantation, • have previously received an organ transplant, • require monitoring for potential organ rejection, or • are planning to have a child or need a blood transfusion.

faqs.question: What if the results of the DSA Test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal DSA Test results may indicate • higher risk of organ rejection due to incompatible HLA antigens, or • presence of antibodies that can cause complications during pregnancy or transfusions.

faqs.question: What to expect during the DSA Test?
faqs.answer: Blood samples will be collected from the recipient and potential donor(s). These samples will be sent for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the DSA Test?
faqs.answer: • Inform your healthcare provider about any medications, supplements, or allergies you have. Also, tell them if you have any specific requirements. • Provide relevant clinical history and complete any required consent forms. • Follow any instructions given by your doctor regarding fasting or medication restrictions prior to the test.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the DSA Test?
faqs.answer: • Crossmatch Test: Identifies if there are antibodies in your blood that could react against the potential donor's cells • Antibody Screening: Helps identify antibodies that may cause complications during pregnancy or blood transfusions • HLA Typing: Determines your tissue type for matching purposes and evaluates compatibility with potential donors

faqs.question: What is the DSA Test also known as?
faqs.answer: HLA Studies or HLA-Special tests

faqs.question: What is organ transplantation?
faqs.answer: Organ transplantation is a surgical procedure where a healthy organ from a donor is placed into a recipient's body to replace a damaged or non-functional organ. It is often performed to treat end-stage organ failure and improve quality of life for individuals with various conditions.

name: Fungal Stain by KOH & Calcofluor White Stain - Sputum

faqs.question: What does the Fungal Stain Test - Sputum measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence of fungi in your sputum sample.

faqs.question: Why is the Fungal Stain Test - Sputum done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose fungal infections in the respiratory tract • To monitor the effectiveness of treatment for fungal infections • To identify specific fungi causing infections for targeted treatment • To assess the risk of developing fungal-related complications

faqs.question: When is Fungal Stain Test - Sputum recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend this test if you • have symptoms suggestive of a fungal respiratory infection, such as persistent cough, chest pain, or difficulty breathing, • have a weakened immune system due to conditions like HIV/AIDS or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy, • have been exposed to environments with high fungal contamination, or • need to monitor the progress of treatment for a known fungal infection.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Fungal Stain Test - Sputum are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate the presence of fungal elements in the sputum, suggesting a fungal respiratory infection.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Fungal Stain Test - Sputum?
faqs.answer: During this test, you will be asked to provide a sputum sample in a sterile, leak-proof container. The sample will be sent to a laboratory for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Fungal Stain Test - Sputum?
faqs.answer: • Follow any additional instructions given by your healthcare provider. • Inform your doctor if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Fungal Stain Test - Sputum?
faqs.answer: • Fungal Culture: This test helps identify the specific type of fungi causing the infection. • Antifungal Susceptibility Testing: It determines which antifungal medications are most effective against the identified fungus.

faqs.question: What is the Fungal Stain by KOH & Calcofluor White Stain also known as?
faqs.answer: KOH & Calcofluor White Stain for fungal elements in sputum

faqs.question: What is a fungal infection?
faqs.answer: A fungal infection is caused by various types of fungi and can affect different parts of the body, including the respiratory tract. Common fungal infections include candidiasis, aspergillosis, and histoplasmosis. Treatment depends on the type and severity of the infection.

faqs.question: What viruses does the Covi-Influenza Viral Panel detect?
faqs.answer: It detects six major respiratory viruses — Influenza A, Influenza B, H1N1, H3N2, RSV, and SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19).

faqs.question: What sample is required for the test?
faqs.answer: A nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swab collected in a VTM tube.

faqs.question: How soon are results available?
faqs.answer: Reports are usually available on the same day once the sample reaches the lab.

faqs.question: Is fasting needed for this test?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required.

faqs.question: Can I take nasal medication before the test?
faqs.answer: Avoid using nasal sprays or decongestants before sample collection.

faqs.question: Can this test differentiate between COVID-19 and flu?
faqs.answer: Yes, it distinguishes between influenza viruses and SARS-CoV-2 infections in a single test.

faqs.question: Who should take this test?
faqs.answer: Anyone with fever, cough, sore throat, or flu-like symptoms, especially during flu or COVID-19 seasons.

faqs.question: Who Should Get MTB Xpert XDR Rapid (Pulmonary) Test Done?
faqs.answer: The test should be recommended to patients in whom MTB infection and possible drug resistance is suspected.

faqs.question: What to expect during MTB Xpert XDR Rapid (Pulmonary) test?

faqs.question: Are any preparations required for MTB Xpert XDR Rapid (Pulmonary) test?

faqs.question: What if results are High/ Low?

name: PSA Total Test
preparation: Avoid the test for 7 days after PR examination and USG. High biotin doses (>5 mg/day) should be avoided at least 8 hours before blood collection. Show More

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the PSA test?
faqs.answer: There is no specific best time of day for a PSA test. However, avoid ejaculation, vigorous exercise like cycling, and digital rectal exams for 48 hours before testing, as these activities can temporarily raise your PSA levels.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the PSA test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required for a PSA test. You can eat and drink normally before the test, as food intake does not affect PSA levels.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my PSA test results?
faqs.answer: Severe dehydration can make your blood more concentrated, potentially leading to falsely elevated results. It's best to maintain normal hydration before any blood test.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the PSA test?
faqs.answer: No special diet is needed before a PSA test. However, it's important to inform your doctor about all medications, like finasteride or dutasteride, and supplements you are taking, including biotin, as some can affect PSA test results.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the PSA test?
faqs.answer: The procedure involves cleaning your arm with an antiseptic, tying an elastic band around your upper arm, inserting a small needle into the vein, and collecting blood in a vial. The entire process takes only a few minutes.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: The risks are minimal and similar to any standard blood test. You might experience slight pain, a small bruise at the needle site, or feel dizzy momentarily. Serious complications like infection are very rare.

faqs.question: What level of PSA test is normal?
faqs.answer: For men aged 59.1-69 years, the PSA test normal range is 0-4.5 ng/mL. However, doctors consider age, prostate size, and rate of change over time

faqs.question: What is the PSA test also known as?
faqs.answer: The PSA test is also known as Total PSA, Serum PSA, or Free Prostate-Specific Antigen when measuring the free component separately. These names refer to the same basic screening test for prostate health.

faqs.question: Can a person have GAD antibodies without diabetes?
faqs.answer: Yes, some individuals may have GAD antibodies due to other autoimmune conditions or as an early predictor of future diabetes.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Skin test are abnormal?

faqs.question: Why is AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Cycloserine Drug by Conventional LJ – Pure Growth of MTB Complex done?
faqs.answer: • This test is primarily done to assess the drug susceptibility of tuberculosis bacteria. • To guide the selection of appropriate medications for tuberculosis treatment • To monitor the effectiveness of ongoing tuberculosis treatment • To identify drug-resistant strains of tuberculosis

faqs.question: When is AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Cycloserine Drug by Conventional LJ – Pure Growth of MTB Complex recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is typically recommended when a person has • A suspected or confirmed diagnosis of tuberculosis • An inadequate response to previous tuberculosis treatment • Symptoms suggestive of drug-resistant tuberculosis • A history of exposure to drug-resistant tuberculosis

faqs.question: What if the results of the AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Cycloserine Drug by Conventional LJ – Pure Growth of MTB Complex are abnormal?

faqs.question: What to expect during the AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Cycloserine Drug by Conventional LJ – Pure Growth of MTB Complex?

faqs.question: What is AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Cycloserine Drug by Conventional LJ – Pure Growth of MTB Complex also known as?

faqs.question: What is tuberculosis?
faqs.answer: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease caused by the bacteria Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It primarily affects the lungs but can also affect other parts of the body. TB spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Early detection and appropriate treatment are crucial to prevent its spread and manage the disease effectively.

faqs.question: What does the Panel Reactive Antibody (PRA) Screening measure?
faqs.answer: This test measures the presence of class I and class II antibodies in your blood.

faqs.question: Why is PRA Screening done?
faqs.answer: • To evaluate the compatibility between an organ donor and recipient prior to transplantation • To assess the level of sensitisation and reduce the risk of organ rejection due to pre-existing antibodies present in the recipient's blood

faqs.question: When is PRA Screening recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend this test if • you are a candidate for organ transplantation or have previously received a transplant, or • you have been exposed to blood transfusions, pregnancies, or previous transplants.

faqs.question: What if the results of PRA Screening are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Increased levels of class I and/or class II antibodies suggest a higher risk of organ rejection due to pre-existing antibodies.

faqs.question: What to expect during PRA Screening?
faqs.answer: During this test, a blood sample will be collected from you. The sample will be sent to the laboratory for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before PRA Screening?
faqs.answer: • Inform your doctor about any medications or supplements you are currently taking. Also, tell them if you have any specific requirements. • Follow your doctor's instructions and inform them about any recent blood transfusions, pregnancies, or previous transplants.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with PRA Screening?
faqs.answer: • Human Leucocyte Antigen (HLA) typing: This test determines the specific genetic markers present on your cells, aiding in transplant matching. • Crossmatch test: This test assesses the compatibility between your antibodies and the potential donor's cells. • Transplant workup tests: These tests evaluate your overall health, including kidney and liver function, to ensure successful transplantation.

faqs.question: What is the Panel Reactive Antibody (PRA) Screening also known as?
faqs.answer: Panel Reactive Antibody testing

faqs.question: What is organ transplantation?
faqs.answer: Organ transplantation is a surgical procedure that involves replacing a diseased or failing organ with a healthy one from a donor. It is primarily performed to treat conditions such as kidney, liver, heart, or lung failure. Transplantation offers improved quality of life and increased survival rates for eligible patients.

faqs.question: What does a positive Hepatitis A Virus (HAV) IgG antibody test indicate?
faqs.answer: A positive or reactive result means you are immune to Hepatitis A due to past infection or vaccination.

faqs.question: What does a negative Hepatitis A Virus (HAV) IgG antibody test mean?
faqs.answer: A negative result indicates no antibodies to Hepatitis A, meaning you are not immune. Vaccination may be needed.

faqs.question: Is fasting required before the Hepatitis A Virus (HAV) IgG antibody test?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required. You can eat and drink normally before your test.

faqs.question: Can the Hepatitis A Virus (HAV) IgG antibody test detect a current infection?
faqs.answer: No, it only shows past infection or immunity. For active infection, your doctor may recommend an HAV IgM test.

faqs.question: Can I take this test after getting the Hepatitis A vaccine?
faqs.answer: Yes, but it’s best to wait at least a few weeks after vaccination to allow antibodies to form for accurate results.

faqs.question: When is the AFB-Smear Examination by Fluorescent Stain – BAL / Other Respiratory Sample recommended and who should take the test?

faqs.question: What if the results of the AFB-Smear Examination by Fluorescent Stain – BAL / Other Respiratory Sample are abnormal?

name: Thyroid Panel 2 Test
preparation: High biotin doses (> 5 mg/day) should be avoided at least 8 hours before blood collection.

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the thyroid panel 2 test?
faqs.answer: The best time for a thyroid panel 2 test is early morning, typically between 8 and 10 AM. TSH levels are naturally highest in the morning, which helps detect mild thyroid issues more accurately and provides consistent results for monitoring.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the thyroid panel 2 test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, overnight fasting is not mandatory for the thyroid panel 2 test. You can eat and drink normally before giving your blood sample. However, if other tests are ordered alongside, your doctor may recommend fasting.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my thyroid panel 2 test results?
faqs.answer: Yes, severe dehydration can concentrate your blood and potentially alter test results slightly. It's best to maintain normal hydration levels before your test by drinking adequate water unless specifically instructed otherwise by your healthcare provider.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the thyroid panel 2 test?
faqs.answer: Continue your regular diet and medications as usual. However, stop high-dose biotin supplements (> 5 mg/day) at least 8 hours before testing, as they can interfere with results. Inform your doctor about all medications you're taking.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the thyroid panel 2 test?
faqs.answer: A trained phlebotomist cleans your arm, ties a band to make veins visible, inserts a small needle into your vein, and collects 3 ml of blood in a special tube. The procedure is quick and minimally uncomfortable.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: The thyroid panel 2 test carries minimal risks similar to any blood draw. You may experience slight pain or bruising at the needle site or, rarely, dizziness or fainting. Infection risk is extremely low with proper sterile techniques.

faqs.question: What level of thyroid panel 2 test is normal?
faqs.answer: Normal ranges are TSH 0.54-5.3 μIU/mL, Free T3 2.0-4.4 pg/mL, and Free T4 0.93-1.7 ng/dL. Speak to your doctor for accurate interpretations of results in the context of your health.

faqs.question: What is the thyroid panel 2 test also known as?
faqs.answer: This test is also known as Thyroid Profile - 2, Thyroid Panel Test - 2 (FT3, FT4, TSH), Comprehensive Thyroid Function Test, or Extended Thyroid Panel.

faqs.question: When is the Fungal Culture and Identification test - Ear recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended for individuals who • have symptoms of a fungal ear infection, such as itching, discharge, pain, or hearing loss, • have not responded to initial treatment for an ear infection, or • are at a higher risk of developing fungal infections, such as those with a weakened immune system or frequent exposure to damp environments.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Fungal Culture and Identification test - Ear are abnormal?

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - Ear?
faqs.answer: • Inform your doctor about any medications you are taking, including topical ear drops. Also, tell them if you have any specific requirements. • Follow any instructions given by your doctor regarding cleaning your ear before the test.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - Ear?

faqs.question: What is a fungal ear infection?

name: Fungal Stain By KOH & Calcofluor White Stain - Specify Type Body Fluid

faqs.question: What does the Fungal Stain Test - Body Fluid measure?
faqs.answer: This test examines body fluid samples to detect the presence of fungi.

faqs.question: Why is the Fungal Stain Test - Body Fluid done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose fungal infections • To guide treatment by monitoring the effectiveness of antifungal medications • To prevent complications through early detection and treatment of fungal infections

faqs.question: When is the Fungal Stain Test - Body Fluid recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: • If you have symptoms such as persistent fever, unexplained weight loss, chronic cough, or skin rashes, your doctor may recommend this test. • If a culture result indicates possible fungal growth, this test can confirm the presence of fungi. • If you are being treated for a fungal infection, this test helps assess treatment effectiveness.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Fungal Stain Test - Body Fluid are abnormal?
faqs.answer: • Positive result: The presence of fungi suggests a fungal infection that needs further evaluation and appropriate treatment. • Negative result: The absence of fungi may indicate that other causes should be considered for your symptoms.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Fungal Stain Test - Body Fluid?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional will collect 3 ml of your body fluid in a sterile, leak-proof container. - Laboratory processing: The sample undergoes staining with specific dyes to detect the presence of fungi. - Reporting: Results are available after 6 hours and will be reported to your doctor.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Fungal Stain Test - Body Fluid?
faqs.answer: - Clinical history: Provide information about your symptoms and medical history to assist in accurate diagnosis. - Sample collection: Collect the body fluid sample in a sterile container as per the given guidelines. - Clinician details: Ensure the specimen type, site, clinical history, and clinician contact number are correctly mentioned on the test request form.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with Fungal Stain Test - Body Fluid?
faqs.answer: Additional tests that may be performed alongside Fungal Stain Test - Body Fluid include: - Culture and Sensitivity Testing: This test helps identify the specific type of fungus causing the infection and determine the most effective treatment. - PCR Testing: Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) is used to detect genetic material of fungi, providing a rapid and accurate diagnosis.

faqs.question: What is the Fungal Stain Test - Body Fluid also known as?

faqs.question: What is a fungal infection?

Common fungal infections include athlete's foot, yeast infections, and pneumonia caused by fungi like Candida and Aspergillus.

faqs.question: Why is the JEV RNA Detection test done?
faqs.answer: • To detect if you have been infected with the Japanese Encephalitis Virus • To monitor the effectiveness of treatment if you have already been diagnosed with JEV

faqs.question: When is the JEV RNA Detection test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend this test if you have • symptoms such as fever, headache, vomiting, seizures, or confusion, • been exposed to mosquitoes in areas where JEV is common, • travelled to an area where JEV is prevalent, or • already been diagnosed with JEV and require further monitoring of the condition.

faqs.question: What if the results of the JEV RNA Detection test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: If the test results are positive, it indicates that JEV is present in your blood and that you have been infected with the virus.

faqs.question: What to expect during the JEV RNA Detection plasma test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional will collect a blood sample from your arm. They will send the sample to the lab for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the JEV RNA Detection test?
faqs.answer: • You may be asked to fast for a few hours before the test. • Inform your doctor about any medications you are taking and any allergies you have. • Inform your doctor if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the JEV RNA Detection test?

faqs.question: What is the JEV RNA Detection by Real-time PCR - EDTA Plasma also known as?
faqs.answer: JEV RT PCR or Japanese Encephalitis Virus Real-Time PCR

faqs.question: What is Japanese Encephalitis?
faqs.answer: Japanese encephalitis is a viral infection caused by the Japanese Encephalitis Virus (JEV). The virus is mainly transmitted by mosquitoes and can cause inflammation in the brain and spinal cord. Common symptoms include fever, headache, seizures, vomiting, and confusion. In severe cases, it can be life-threatening.
