name: JEV RNA Detection by Real-time PCR - Serum

faqs.question: What does JEV RNA Detection by Real-time PCR - Serum measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence of Japanese encephalitis virus RNA (Ribonucleic acid) in serum.

faqs.question: Why is the JEV RNA Detection test done?
faqs.answer: • To detect the presence of JEV in patients with acute encephalitis syndrome, especially during outbreaks in endemic areas • To distinguish Japanese encephalitis from other encephalitides caused by viruses such as dengue, chikungunya, and Zika

faqs.question: When is the JEV RNA Detection test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended for patients with suspected Japanese encephalitis, especially if they live in or have recently visited endemic areas. Pregnant women and immunocompromised patients are at higher risk.

faqs.question: What if the results of the JEV RNA Detection test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: A positive result indicates that the patient has an active JEV infection. Other possible causes of positive results include cross-reactivity with related flaviviruses or prior vaccination.

faqs.question: What to expect during the JEV RNA Detection Serum test?
faqs.answer: The test involves drawing a 3 ml blood sample from a vein in your arm and sending it to the laboratory for processing.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the JEV RNA Detection test?
faqs.answer: Inform your doctor if you have taken any antiviral medications or received any vaccinations against JEV or related flaviviruses. Also, let them know if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the JEV RNA Detection test?
faqs.answer: • Serum IgM antibody testing: To detect recent JEV infection • Cerebrospinal fluid analysis: To assess brain inflammation and rule out other causes of encephalitis

faqs.question: What is JEV RNA Detection by Real-time PCR - Serum also known as?
faqs.answer: EV RT-PCR or Japanese encephalitis PCR

faqs.question: What is Japanese Encephalitis?
faqs.answer: Japanese encephalitis is a mosquito-borne viral disease that affects the brain. It can cause severe illness and death. Vaccination is an effective preventive measure for those living in or travelling to endemic areas.

name: Culture & Sensitivity, Aerobic bacteria Central Line Catheter Tip

faqs.question: Why is Culture & Sensitivity, Aerobic bacteria - Central Line Catheter Tip test done?
faqs.answer: This test is done to find the causative agent of bacteraemia from central line tip culture. The test also establishes the antibiotics that can be used against the isolated causative agent.

faqs.question: What does it measure?
faqs.answer: This test establishes presence or absence bacteria on the central line tip. In case bacterium is isolated then antibiotic susceptibility testing is also done.

faqs.question: What to expect during the test?
faqs.answer: This test tip of the central line. Sample is collected by the doctor and send to lab in sterile container

faqs.question: What are the normal levels?
faqs.answer: No growth

faqs.question: What if results are Present/ Absent?
faqs.answer: No growth: This means that bacterium could not be isolated from the tip Significant Growth: This means that bacterium was isolated from the sample (?15 cfu). The sensitivity of the bacterium towards various antibiotics is also reported. The result have to be correlated clinically in case a skin commensal is isolated.

name: BCR-ABL Breakpoint Analysis Qualitative By Real Time PCR - Bone Marrow

faqs.question: What does BCR-ABL Breakpoint Analysis measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the breakpoints (major, minor, and micro translocations) of BCR-ABL fusion gene.

faqs.question: Why is BCR-ABL Breakpoint Analysis done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose CML • To detect major, minor, and micro translocations of BCR-ABL • To assess the effectiveness of treatment for CML • To guide targeted therapy decisions • To monitor disease progression and response to treatment

faqs.question: When is BCR-ABL Breakpoint Analysis recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended for individuals who • are suspected to have CML, • have symptoms such as fatigue, unexplained weight loss, or enlarged spleen, or • are undergoing treatment for CML to assess response and monitor treatment effectiveness.

faqs.question: What if the results of the BCR-ABL Breakpoint Analysis are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate the presence of major, minor, or micro translocations of BCR-ABL associated with CML.

faqs.question: What to expect during the BCR-ABL Breakpoint Analysis?
faqs.answer: A 3 ml bone marrow sample will be collected in an EDTA Vacutainer. The sample will be sent to the laboratory for processing through the Real-time PCR method.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the BCR-ABL Breakpoint Analysis?
faqs.answer: • No dietary restrictions or specific preparations are required before this test. • Inform your doctor if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with BCR-ABL Breakpoint Analysis?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside BCR-ABL Breakpoint Analysis include • Complete blood count (CBC) • Peripheral blood smear examination • Other molecular tests for specific genetic mutations associated with hematological malignancies

faqs.question: What is the BCR-ABL Breakpoint Analysis also known as?
faqs.answer: BCR-ABL Fusion Gene Analysis

faqs.question: What is Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia?
faqs.answer: Chronic myeloid leukaemia is a type of cancer that affects the white blood cells. It is charactersed by the abnormal fusion of two genes, BCR and ABL, resulting in the production of a protein called BCR-ABL. CML leads to an overproduction of abnormal white blood cells.

name: Alpha N-Acetyl Galactosaminidase Test/ Schindler Disease Test

faqs.question: What does the CA 15.3 Test measure?
faqs.answer: It measures Cancer Antigen 15-3 levels in blood to support monitoring of breast cancer treatment response, progression, and recurrence.

faqs.question: Do I need to fast before this test?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required.

faqs.question: Can the CA 15.3 Test detect breast cancer early?
faqs.answer: No. It is not a screening test and is primarily used for monitoring in patients with known breast cancer.

faqs.question: What does a high CA 15.3 level mean?
faqs.answer: It may suggest recurrence or metastasis in breast cancer, but it can also rise in benign conditions; clinical correlation and further testing are needed.

faqs.question: Can men take the CA 15.3 Test?
faqs.answer: Yes. Although commonly used in breast cancer monitoring, CA 15-3 may be elevated in other cancers as well.

faqs.question: Which method is used for this test?
faqs.answer: The test is commonly performed using Electrochemiluminescence Immunoassay (ECLIA).

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the peripheral smear test?
faqs.answer: There is no specific best time for a peripheral smear test. You can take this test at any time of the day that's convenient for you, as timing doesn't affect the results.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the peripheral smear test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required for a peripheral smear test alone. You can eat and drink normally before the test unless other blood tests requiring fasting are ordered simultaneously.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my peripheral smear test results?
faqs.answer: Yes, severe dehydration can cause blood concentration changes that may affect cell counts and appearance. It's recommended to stay well-hydrated before any blood test for accurate results.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the peripheral smear test?
faqs.answer: No special dietary preparation is needed. However, inform your doctor about all medications, vitamins, and supplements you're taking, as some drugs can affect blood cell appearance or counts.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the peripheral smear test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional cleans your arm, inserts a sterile needle into a vein, and draws a small blood sample into an EDTA tube. The procedure is quick and minimally uncomfortable.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: Risks are minimal and include slight pain at the needle site, minor bruising, or light-headedness. Serious complications, like infection, are extremely rare with proper sterile technique.

faqs.question: What level of peripheral smear test is normal?
faqs.answer: A normal peripheral smear report describes blood cells as normal in size, shape, and appearance, with no abnormal cells or parasites seen. Results are descriptive rather than numerical values.

faqs.question: What is the peripheral smear test also known as?
faqs.answer: The test is also called Peripheral Blood Film (PBF), Blood Smear Analysis, Manual Differential, or PBS (Peripheral Smear Examination).

name: AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Body Fluid

faqs.question: What does the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Body Fluid test measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Non-tuberculous Mycobacteria (NTM) in body fluid samples.

faqs.question: Why is the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Body Fluid test done?
faqs.answer: This test is done to • Diagnose infections caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis or NTM. • Monitor the effectiveness of treatment for tuberculosis. • Identify the presence of other mycobacterial infections.

faqs.question: When is the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Body Fluid test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended if you • Have symptoms suggestive of tuberculosis, such as persistent cough, weight loss, fever, and night sweats. • Have been exposed to someone with tuberculosis. • Have a weakened immune system. • Are being treated for tuberculosis and need monitoring.

faqs.question: What if the results of the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Body Fluid test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate an active infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis or other non-tuberculous mycobacteria.

faqs.question: What to expect during the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Body Fluid test?
faqs.answer: During this test, a 2ml sample of your body fluids will be collected in a sterile container and it will be sent to the laboratory for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Body Fluid test?
faqs.answer: To prepare for this test: • Ensure that the specimen type, site, and proper clinical history are mentioned on the Test Request Form (TRF). • Collect 2ml of body fluid in a sterile container. • Follow any fasting or medication instructions given by your doctor. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Body Fluid test?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Body Fluid test include: • AFB Smear Microscopy: This test quickly identifies acid-fast bacilli in clinical samples. • GeneXpert MTB/RIF Assay: This molecular test detects the presence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis and drug resistance. • Chest X-ray: Imaging test used to detect abnormalities in the lungs suggestive of tuberculosis infection.

faqs.question: What is the AFB Rapid Culture by MGIT – Body Fluid test also known as?
faqs.answer: Acid-Fast Bacillus Rapid Culture by Mycobacteria Growth Indicator Tube

faqs.question: What is tuberculosis?
faqs.answer: Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It primarily affects the lungs but can also affect other parts of the body. Symptoms include cough, weight loss, and fatigue.

faqs.question: What does the Ceruloplasmin Test measure?
faqs.answer: It measures the level of ceruloplasmin, a copper-carrying protein made by your liver, to assess copper metabolism and liver function.

faqs.question: What does a low ceruloplasmin level mean?
faqs.answer: Low levels often suggest Wilson’s disease, Menkes disease, malnutrition, or severe liver dysfunction.

faqs.question: What causes high ceruloplasmin levels?
faqs.answer: High levels can occur due to inflammation, infections, pregnancy, or while taking oral contraceptives.

faqs.question: Do I need to fast before the Ceruloplasmin Test?
faqs.answer: Fasting not required. You can eat and drink normally before the test.

faqs.question: Can medications affect the results?
faqs.answer: Yes, certain drugs like oral contraceptives, hormone therapies, or zinc supplements may influence ceruloplasmin readings.

faqs.question: How is the Ceruloplasmin Test done?
faqs.answer: A small blood sample is drawn from your arm and tested using Immunoturbidimetry to measure ceruloplasmin levels.

faqs.question: Can this test detect Wilson’s disease?
faqs.answer: Yes, low ceruloplasmin levels are a key indicator of Wilson’s disease, especially when combined with copper tests.

faqs.question: How long will it take to receive my results?
faqs.answer: Reports are generally available within 6 hours once your sample reaches the lab.

faqs.question: Why is Anti MAG (Myelin associated Glycoprotein) Ab (M0001) test done?
faqs.answer: Anti MAG (Myelin associated Glycoprotein) antibody test is used for evaluating peripheral neuropathy and paraproteinemic neuropathy. The presence of MAG antibodies is not a complete diagnostic test of an acquired neuropathy and results must be interpreted with clinical and electrophysiological tests.

faqs.question: What does it measure?
faqs.answer: The test measures the concentration of autoantibodies to MAG.

faqs.question: What to expect during the test?
faqs.answer: This test requires a blood sample. A tourniquet (elastic) band is placed tightly on the upper arm. The patient is then asked to make a fist. This helps in the build-up of blood filling the veins. The skin is disinfected before needle insertion and the blood sample is collected in vacutainer.

faqs.question: What if results are Present/ Absent?
faqs.answer: High levels of MAG antibodies may indicate active demyelination in peripheral neuropathies associated with MAG. Low levels may rule out MAG associated peripheral neuropathy but can be associated with other types of neuropathies. Results should be correlated with clinical and electrophysiological findings as well.

name: TSH Test (Ultrasensitive
preparation: Clinical history is required; high biotin doses (> 5 mg/day) should be avoided at least 8 hours before blood collection. Show More

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the TSH test?
faqs.answer: TSH levels naturally fluctuate throughout the day and are highest in the early morning. While you can take the test anytime, morning collection is often recommended for consistency, especially when monitoring treatment.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the TSH test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required for a standalone TSH test. You can eat and drink normally before the test. However, if combined with other tests, your doctor may provide specific fasting instructions.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my TSH test results?
faqs.answer: Mild dehydration typically doesn't significantly impact TSH results, but severe dehydration may affect blood test accuracy by concentrating blood components. Stay normally hydrated before testing.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the TSH test?
faqs.answer: No special diet is needed. However, stop high-dose biotin supplements (> 5 mg/day) at least 8 hours before testing. Inform your doctor about all medications you're taking, as some may affect results.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the TSH test?
faqs.answer: A trained phlebotomist cleans your arm, applies a tourniquet, and inserts a small needle into a vein to collect blood. The procedure is quick and minimally uncomfortable.

faqs.question: What level of TSH test is normal?
faqs.answer: Normal TSH levels typically range from 0.54 to 5.3 μIU/mL, though this may vary slightly between laboratories. Your doctor will interpret results based on your individual health status.

faqs.question: What is the TSH test also known as?
faqs.answer: The TSH Test is also known as the Thyrotropin Test, the TSH Ultrasensitive Test, or the TSH-U Test.

faqs.question: Is the TSH 3rd-generation test painful?
faqs.answer: The test is not painful. You may feel a slight prick when the needle enters your arm, but this brief discomfort lasts only a few seconds and is generally well-tolerated by most people.

faqs.question: What foods reduce thyroid?
faqs.answer: Foods that may reduce thyroid function include soy products, cruciferous vegetables (like broccoli and cabbage), processed foods, and those high in gluten, especially for people with autoimmune thyroid disorders. Always consult your doctor for personalised dietary advice.

faqs.question: What does it mean if your TSH 3rd-generation is high?
faqs.answer: High TSH levels (above 5.3 μIU/mL) typically indicate hypothyroidism, meaning your thyroid gland isn't producing enough hormones, prompting your pituitary gland to release more TSH.

faqs.question: What does the Fungal Culture and Identification – Urine test measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence of fungi in urine samples.

faqs.question: Why is the Fungal Culture and Identification – Urine test done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose fungal infections in the urinary tract • To determine the specific type of fungus causing the infection • To guide appropriate antifungal treatment • To monitor the effectiveness of antifungal therapy • To assess the need for ongoing treatment or follow-up care

faqs.question: When is the Fungal Culture and Identification – Urine test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended for individuals who • Have symptoms of a urinary tract infection that hasn't responded to antibiotics. • Are at a higher risk of developing fungal infections, such as those with weakened immune systems or prolonged antibiotic use. • Need to monitor the effectiveness of antifungal treatment for a urinary tract infection.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Fungal Culture and Identification – Urine test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate the presence of a fungal infection in the urinary tract.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Fungal Culture and Identification – Urine test?
faqs.answer: You will be asked to provide a spot urine sample in a sterile container. The sample will be sent to the laboratory for fungal culture and identification.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Fungal Culture and Identification – Urine test?
faqs.answer: • Avoid urinating for at least two hours before collecting the urine sample. • Collect a fresh, random urine sample in a sterile, leak-proof container. • Ensure that your name, specimen type, site, clinical history, and clinician's contact information are properly mentioned on the test request form. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Fungal Culture and Identification – Urine test?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside the Fungal Culture and Identification – Urine test include: • Blood tests to assess overall health and immune function • Additional cultures or tests to check for other types of infections • Imaging tests such as ultrasound or CT scan to evaluate the urinary tract for any abnormalities

faqs.question: What is the Fungal Culture and Identification – Urine test also known as?
faqs.answer: Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) Urine

faqs.question: What is a fungal infection in the urinary tract?
faqs.answer: A fungal infection in the urinary tract is caused by the overgrowth of fungi, such as Candida or Aspergillus species. It can affect different parts of the urinary system and may cause symptoms such as frequent urination, pain during urination, or blood in the urine.

name: Beta HCG Subunit Test
preparation: High biotin doses (> 5 mg/day) should be avoided at least 8 hrs before blood collection. Mention LMP, USG findings or other clinical history. Show More

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the beta HCG test?
faqs.answer: NULL

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the beta HCG test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required for the beta HCG test. You can eat and drink normally before the test unless your doctor specifically advises otherwise, if other tests requiring fasting are being done simultaneously.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my beta HCG test results?
faqs.answer: Dehydration is unlikely to significantly affect bHCG test results. While severe dehydration can affect blood concentration, it's not considered a factor that would invalidate the test result. Dehydration affects urine tests more than blood tests.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the beta HCG test?
faqs.answer: No special dietary preparations are needed. However, inform your doctor about all medications you're taking, including biotin supplements.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the beta HCG test?
faqs.answer: The procedure involves tying an elastic band around your upper arm, cleaning the area with antiseptic, inserting a small needle into a vein to collect blood into a vial, then removing the needle and applying a bandage.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: The risks are minimal and similar to any standard blood test. These may include slight pain or bruising at the needle site, feeling lightheaded or dizzy, and a very small risk of infection at the puncture site.

faqs.question: What level of beta HCG test is normal?
faqs.answer: Normal levels vary widely depending on pregnancy status and gestational age. Non-pregnant women typically have levels below 5.3 mIU/mL, while pregnant women's levels range from 5.8 mIU/mL at 3 weeks to over 180,000 mIU/mL at 10 weeks of pregnancy.

faqs.question: What is the beta HCG test also known as?
faqs.answer: The beta HCG test is also known as the HCG Beta Subunit Test, Quantitative hCG Test, hCG Blood Test, Quantitative Serum Beta-hCG Test, and Total hCG Test, all referring to the same blood test.

name: HAV IgM Test - Hepatitis A Virus IgM Antibody
preparation: Clinical history and clinician contact details required

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the HAV IgM Test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend the test when you have symptoms of acute hepatitis, such as jaundice, fever, nausea, abdominal pain or dark urine. HAV IgM is usually detectable around the onset of symptoms.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the HAV IgM Test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, overnight fasting is not required. You can eat and drink normally before the test.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my HAV IgM Test results?
faqs.answer: Mild dehydration is unlikely to directly affect HAV IgM antibody detection, but normal hydration makes blood collection easier and more comfortable.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the HAV IgM Test?
faqs.answer: No special diet is needed. Inform your doctor about all medicines, supplements and ongoing treatments you are taking.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the HAV IgM Test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional ties a tourniquet around your arm, cleans the puncture site, inserts a sterile needle into a vein and collects about 3 ml of blood in a gel vacutainer.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: The risks are minimal and similar to a routine blood test. You may feel slight pain, mild bruising or temporary swelling at the needle site. Rarely, some people may feel dizzy.

faqs.question: What level of HAV IgM Test is normal?
faqs.answer: A COI less than 1.0 is considered non-reactive. A COI greater than or equal to 1.0 is considered reactive and should be interpreted by your doctor with your symptoms and liver function test results.

faqs.question: What does the Acid Phosphatase Total measure?
faqs.answer: This test measures the concentration of acid phosphatase enzymes in the serum.

faqs.question: Why is the Acid Phosphatase Total test done?
faqs.answer: • The test is typically performed to assess prostate health and diagnose conditions such as prostate cancer and benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). • Elevated acid phosphatase levels may indicate prostate gland abnormalities. • To diagnose prostatic cancer metastasis

faqs.question: When is the Acid Phosphatase Total recommended, and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended for individuals when there is suspicion of prostate-related conditions, especially in those with symptoms like urinary problems, elevated prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, or a family history of prostate cancer.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Acid Phosphatase Total test are positive?
faqs.answer: A positive result may indicate elevated acid phosphatase levels in the serum, suggesting the possibility of prostate gland abnormalities.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Acid Phosphatase Total test?
faqs.answer: The test involves a blood draw, where a healthcare professional collects a serum sample from a vein, typically in the arm. The procedure is minimally invasive and relatively quick.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Acid Phosphatase Total test?
faqs.answer: Patients typically do not need specific preparations before the test. However, it's important to follow any instructions provided by the healthcare provider.

faqs.question: Which other tests are ordered with the Acid Phosphatase Total test?
faqs.answer: The Acid Phosphatase Total Serum test is often part of a comprehensive evaluation for prostate health. Additional tests may include PSA testing, digital rectal examination (DRE), and prostate biopsies.

faqs.question: What is the Acid Phosphatase Total test also known as?
faqs.answer: The Acid Phosphatase Total Serum test may also be referred to as the serum acid phosphatase test.

name: Fungal stain by KOH & Calcofluor White stain - BAL /E.T Secretion/Respiratory Sample

faqs.question: What does the Fungal Stain Test - BAL/ET Secretion/Respiratory Sample measure?
faqs.answer: The Fungal Stain Test detects the presence of fungal elements in respiratory samples, such as bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) or other respiratory secretions.

faqs.question: Why is the Fungal Stain Test - BAL/ET Secretion/Respiratory Sample done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose fungal infections in the respiratory system • To determine the appropriate treatment for patients with suspected fungal infections

faqs.question: When is the Fungal Stain Test - BAL/ET Secretion/Respiratory Sample recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: The Fungal Stain Test may be recommended if you have symptoms such as persistent cough, shortness of breath, recurrent lung infections, or other signs of respiratory infection. It is also recommended for individuals at higher risk of fungal infections due to underlying conditions or weakened immune systems.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Fungal Stain Test - BAL/ET Secretion/Respiratory Sample are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may suggest a fungal infection. However, further tests and clinical evaluation are necessary to confirm the diagnosis and determine the appropriate treatment and management plan.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Fungal Stain Test- BAL/ET Secretion/Respiratory Sample?
faqs.answer: During the test, a healthcare professional will draw your respiratory sample such as BAL or other secretions. They will send the sample for analysis using the stains KOH and Calcofluor White

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Fungal Stain Test- BAL/ET Secretion/Respiratory Sample?
faqs.answer: • No specific dietary or medication restrictions are necessary before this test. • Inform your doctor if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Fungal Stain Test- BAL/ET Secretion/Respiratory Sample?
faqs.answer: • Microbiology Culture: To identify the specific type of fungus causing the infection • Antifungal Susceptibility Testing: To determine which antifungal medications are most effective against the identified fungus • PCR Testing: To detect the presence of specific fungal DNA in the respiratory sample

faqs.question: What is the Fungal Stain Test - BAL/ET Secretion/Respiratory Sample also known as?
faqs.answer: Respiratory Fungal Stain Test

faqs.question: What is a fungal infection?
faqs.answer: Fungal infections are caused by various types of fungi and can affect different parts of the body, including the respiratory system. They can cause symptoms such as coughing, wheezing, and fever. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are important for managing fungal infections effectively.

name: DNA (Double Strand) AntibodyNcX DNASerum - DS DNA CTX Test

faqs.question: What is the anti-double stranded DNA test used for?
faqs.answer: It is used to diagnose and monitor lupus by detecting antibodies that attack the body’s own DNA.

faqs.question: How is the anti-dsDNA test performed?
faqs.answer: A small blood sample is collected from your vein and analysed using the Enzyme Immunoassay method.

faqs.question: Do I need to fast before the test?
faqs.answer: No fasting is required before this test.

faqs.question: What does a high anti-dsDNA antibody level mean?
faqs.answer: It may indicate active lupus or lupus nephritis, especially during a flare-up.

faqs.question: Can this test confirm lupus?
faqs.answer: Yes, it helps confirm lupus when combined with clinical symptoms and a positive ANA test.

faqs.question: Can other diseases cause a positive result?
faqs.answer: Occasionally, other autoimmune or liver conditions such as Sjögren’s syndrome or autoimmune hepatitis may cause a positive result.

faqs.question: How often should lupus patients take this test?
faqs.answer: Lupus patients may be advised to repeat this test regularly to monitor disease activity and treatment response.

faqs.question: What is the C4 Blood Test used for?
faqs.answer: It measures Complement C4 protein levels to assess immune system and autoimmune conditions.

faqs.question: Is fasting required before the C4 Blood Test?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required.

faqs.question: How is the C4 Blood Test performed?
faqs.answer: A small blood sample is taken from your arm and tested using Immunoturbidimetry.

faqs.question: What does a low C4 level mean?
faqs.answer: It can indicate active autoimmune disease, infection, or complement deficiency.

faqs.question: What does a high C4 level mean?
faqs.answer: It may suggest recovery from infection or ongoing inflammation.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get the report?
faqs.answer: Reports are available within 6 hours after sample reaching the lab.

name: AFB (TB) - Antibiogram For MTb Complex - Streptomycin Drug By MGIT - Pure Growth Of MTB Complex

faqs.question: What does AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Streptomycin measure?
faqs.answer: This test measures the susceptibility of Tuberculosis bacteria to Streptomycin.

faqs.question: Why is AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Streptomycin done?
faqs.answer: • To identify the susceptibility of Tuberculosis bacteria to Streptomycin • To guide doctors in selecting appropriate medications for treating TB • To monitor the effectiveness of ongoing TB treatment • To prevent the development of drug-resistant TB strains

faqs.question: When is AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Streptomycin recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Doctors may recommend this test if • you have been diagnosed with Tuberculosis, • your symptoms persist despite ongoing treatment, • there is a risk of developing drug-resistant Tuberculosis, or • they want to ensure the most effective medication for your specific TB strain.

faqs.question: What if the results of the AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Streptomycin are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate drug-resistant TB, which requires alternative medications for effective treatment.

faqs.question: What to expect during the AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Streptomycin?
faqs.answer: During this test, a healthcare professional will take a sample of your Tuberculosis bacteria. They will test this sample against Streptomycin to determine susceptibility.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Streptomycin?
faqs.answer: • Provide relevant clinical history and clinician contact information for notification. • Follow any other instructions provided by your doctor or the testing facility. • Inform your doctor if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Streptomycin?
faqs.answer: • AFB Stain: This test detects the presence of Acid-Fast Bacilli, confirming the diagnosis of Tuberculosis • GeneXpert MTB/RIF: This molecular diagnostic test identifies both Tuberculosis and Rifampicin resistance simultaneously

faqs.question: What is the AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Streptomycin also known as?
faqs.answer: TB Drug Susceptibility Test - Streptomycin or Mycobacterial Antibiotic Sensitivity Testing - Streptomycin

faqs.question: What is Tuberculosis?
faqs.answer: Tuberculosis (TB) is a bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It primarily affects the lungs but can also impact other organs. TB is transmitted through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial for effective management of TB.

name: Free Testosterone Test
preparation:
Age and gender are required. High biotin doses (>5 mg/day) should be avoided for at least 8 hours before blood collection
Show More

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the testosterone free test?
faqs.answer: The best time for your blood sample is in the morning, when testosterone levels are naturally at their peak for the most accurate results.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the testosterone free test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No fasting is required for the free testosterone test. You can eat and drink normally before your blood collection appointment without affecting the test results.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my testosterone free test results?
faqs.answer: Yes, severe dehydration can concentrate your blood, potentially leading to falsely elevated testosterone readings. Maintain normal hydration by drinking adequate water before your test.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the testosterone free test?
faqs.answer: No special dietary changes are needed. However, inform your doctor about all medications and supplements, especially high-dose biotin, which should be avoided 8 hours before testing.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the testosterone free test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional cleans your arm, ties a band around your upper arm to make veins visible, and then inserts a small needle to collect blood into a tube.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: The risks are minimal, similar to any blood test. You might experience slight pain, minor bruising at the needle site, or, rarely, dizziness during the procedure.

faqs.question: What level of testosterone free test is normal?
faqs.answer: Normal free testosterone ranges are 0.2-4.1 pg/mL. Your doctor will interpret results based on your age, gender, and clinical symptoms.

faqs.question: What does the TNF Alpha Test detect?
faqs.answer: It measures the amount of Tumour Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-α) in your blood, a marker of inflammation linked to autoimmune diseases, infection, and immune activity.

faqs.question: What does a high TNF Alpha level mean?
faqs.answer: Elevated levels usually indicate ongoing inflammation due to autoimmune disease, infection, cancer, or organ rejection.

faqs.question: Do I need to fast before the TNF Alpha Test?
faqs.answer: No fasting is required. You can eat and drink as usual before the test.

faqs.question: Can medications affect my TNF Alpha Test results?
faqs.answer: Yes. Anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive medications may alter TNF-alpha levels. Inform your doctor about all ongoing treatments.

faqs.question: Is the TNF Alpha Test used in cancer monitoring?
faqs.answer: Yes. It helps assess tumour-related inflammation and monitor disease progression in some cancers.

faqs.question: Are there risks associated with the test?
faqs.answer: Risks are minimal and similar to any blood test, including mild discomfort or bruising at the needle site.

faqs.question: What is the purpose of a vaginal culture and sensitivity test?

faqs.question: Can I take the test during my period?
faqs.answer: It is best to avoid testing during menstruation as it may affect accuracy.

faqs.question: Should I stop antibiotics before the test?
faqs.answer: Yes—avoid antibiotics for 48–72 hours before testing unless your doctor advises otherwise.

faqs.question: Is fasting required?
faqs.answer: No. You can eat and drink normally before your appointment.

faqs.question: Is the test painful?
faqs.answer: The swab collection is usually not painful; you may feel brief mild discomfort.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get results?
faqs.answer: Results are usually available after 4 days once the sample reaches the lab.

faqs.question: Can I book home sample collection for this test?
faqs.answer: No. In-lab collection is required due to sterile swab handling and technique requirements.

faqs.question: What does the Mycobacterial Identification Test measure?
faqs.answer: The Mycobacterial Identification Test identifies different species of Mycobacteria present in your sample.

faqs.question: Why is the Mycobacterial Identification Test done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose tuberculosis and other mycobacterial infections • To determine the species of Mycobacteria causing the infection • To assess drug resistance patterns • To monitor treatment progress and effectiveness • To prevent further transmission of the disease

faqs.question: When is the Mycobacterial Identification Test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: The Mycobacterial Identification Test is recommended when you • have symptoms suggestive of tuberculosis or mycobacterial infections, such as persistent cough, fever, weight loss, and night sweats, • are at high risk of tuberculosis due to close contact with an infected individual, or • have a positive result on preliminary tests for mycobacterial infections.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Mycobacterial Identification Test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results from the Mycobacterial Identification Test may indicate • active tuberculosis infection caused by specific species of Mycobacteria, • drug resistance, which may require alternative medication options, or • need for further diagnostic tests.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Mycobacterial Identification Test?
faqs.answer: During the test, a sample of pure growth of Mycobacteria will be collected from your sputum, tissue, or other relevant sources. The sample will be sent to the laboratory, where a technique called MALDI TOF (Vitek MS) will be used for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Mycobacterial Identification Test?
faqs.answer: • Follow any additional instructions provided by your doctor or the laboratory regarding fasting or discontinuing specific medications. • Inform your doctor if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Mycobacterial Identification Test?
faqs.answer: • Acid-Fast Bacillus (AFB) smear: This microscopic examination detects acid-fast bacteria in a patient's sample and is often used as an initial screening test for tuberculosis and other mycobacterial infections. • Gene Xpert MTB/RIF: This molecular test detects the presence of tuberculosis bacteria and determines resistance to rifampicin, an important anti-tuberculosis drug.

faqs.question: What is the Mycobacterial Identification Test also known as?
faqs.answer: Mycobacterial culture identification or mycobacterial species identification

faqs.question: What is tuberculosis?
faqs.answer: Tuberculosis (TB) is a contagious bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It primarily affects the lungs but can also affect other parts of the body. Common symptoms include cough, fever, weight loss, and fatigue.

faqs.question: Why take Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 12 (SCA12) DNA Test?

faqs.question: What does the Factor V Leiden Mutation Test detect?
faqs.answer: It detects the G1691A mutation in the F5 gene that increases the risk of abnormal blood clots.

faqs.question: Why is this test important?
faqs.answer: It helps diagnose hereditary thrombophilia and assess the risk of DVT or PE.

faqs.answer: A 3 ml EDTA blood sample is required.

faqs.question: Do I need to fast before the test?

name: Fungal Culture And Identification Test By MALDITOF (Vitek MS) - CSF

faqs.question: What does the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - CSF measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence of fungal pathogens in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which indicates a fungal infection.

faqs.question: Why is the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - CSF done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose fungal infections in the central nervous system • To identify the type of fungus causing the infection • To assess the effectiveness of antifungal treatment • To guide further management and monitoring of fungal infections

faqs.question: When is the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - CSF recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended for • patients with persistent headaches, fever, neck stiffness, confusion, or altered mental status, • individuals with known risk factors for fungal infections, including immunosuppression or recent organ transplantation, • patients on long-term corticosteroid therapy or receiving chemotherapy, or • those with a history of previous fungal infections or exposure to contaminated environments.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - CSF are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate the presence of a fungal infection in the central nervous system.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - CSF?
faqs.answer: During the test, a healthcare professional will draw a small amount of cerebrospinal fluid from your body in a sterile, leak-proof container. They will send this sample to the laboratory for processing.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - CSF?
faqs.answer: • Follow any instructions given by your doctor regarding fasting or medication restrictions. • Inform your doctor if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - CSF?
faqs.answer: • Blood cultures: To detect systemic fungal infections or determine the source of infection • CSF analysis: To evaluate cell count, glucose, protein levels, and detect other microorganisms • Fungal PCR Testing: To identify specific fungal DNA or RNA in the CSF sample • Antifungal Susceptibility Testing: To determine the most effective antifungal treatment

faqs.question: What is the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - CSF also known as?
faqs.answer: CSF Fungal Culture and Identification or CSF Mycology Test

faqs.question: What is meningitis?
faqs.answer: Meningitis is an inflammatory condition affecting the protective membranes covering the brain and spinal cord. It can be caused by various pathogens, including bacteria, viruses, or fungi. Symptoms include severe headaches, fever, neck stiffness, and sensitivity to light. Immediate medical attention is essential.

faqs.question: What does B-ALL MRD Test measure?
faqs.answer: The B-ALL MRD test analyzes and quantifies the residual leukemic cells in the bone marrow or peripheral blood.

faqs.question: Why is the B-ALL MRD Test done?
faqs.answer: • To assess the presence and level of minimal residual disease (MRD) in patients with B-ALL • To evaluate treatment effectiveness • To monitor disease progression and relapse risk • To guide treatment decisions, such as the need for further therapy or stem cell transplantation

faqs.question: When is B-ALL MRD Test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: The B-ALL MRD test is typically recommended for individuals who have been diagnosed with B-ALL. Patients who may benefit from this test include • those undergoing treatment for B-ALL, • individuals who have completed treatment to assess their response, and • patients at risk of relapse or with suspected disease recurrence.

faqs.question: What if the results of the B-ALL MRD Test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results indicating a high level of MRD may suggest a higher risk of relapse or insufficient response to treatment.

faqs.question: What to expect during the B-ALL MRD Test?
faqs.answer: During the test, a sample of bone marrow will be collected using a needle. The sample will then be sent to the laboratory for analysis using flow cytometry.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the B-ALL MRD Test?
faqs.answer: • Inform your doctor about any medications or supplements you are taking. Also, tell them if you have any specific requirements. • Follow any dietary instructions provided by your doctor.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the B-ALL MRD Test?
faqs.answer: • Complete Blood Count (CBC): Helps evaluate overall blood cell count and health • Bone Marrow Aspiration and Biopsy: Provides detailed information about the structure and function of bone marrow cells • Cytogenetic Testing: Identifies specific genetic changes or abnormalities in cancer cells

faqs.question: What is the B-ALL MRD Test also known as?
faqs.answer: Minimal Residual Disease test for B-Cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia

faqs.question: What is B-Cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia?
faqs.answer: B-Cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia is a type of blood cancer that affects the white blood cells, specifically B-cells. It is characterised by the rapid production of immature lymphoblasts in the bone marrow, which overcrowd normal blood cells and impair their normal function.

faqs.question: What does the AFB-Smear Examination by Fluorescent Stain – Tissue/Biopsy measure?
faqs.answer: This test measures the presence of acid-fast bacilli (AFB) specific to Mycobacterium tuberculosis in tissue or biopsy samples.

faqs.question: Why is AFB-Smear Examination by Fluorescent Stain – Tissue/Biopsy done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose infection caused by tuberculosis • To monitor the effectiveness of tuberculosis treatment • To detect drug resistance in tuberculosis • To rule out tuberculosis infection in individuals with symptoms or risk factors

faqs.question: When is AFB-Smear Examination by Fluorescent Stain – Tissue/Biopsy recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test may be recommended if you • Have symptoms suggestive of tuberculosis, such as persistent cough, weight loss, and night sweats. • Have been exposed to someone with active tuberculosis. • Are at a higher risk of developing tuberculosis, such as individuals with weakened immune systems or certain medical conditions.

faqs.question: What if the results of the AFB-Smear Examination by Fluorescent Stain – Tissue/Biopsy are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results, i.e., results indicating the presence of acid-fast bacilli in the tissue or biopsy sample may indicate an active tuberculosis infection.

faqs.question: What to expect during the AFB-Smear Examination by Fluorescent Stain – Tissue/Biopsy?
faqs.answer: • A tissue or biopsy sample will be taken from the affected area, such as lungs or lymph nodes. • The sample will be processed and stained with a fluorescent dye for examination under a fluorescent microscope.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the AFB-Smear Examination by Fluorescent Stain – Tissue/Biopsy?
faqs.answer: • Inform your doctor about any ongoing medications or allergies. • The specific site and type of tissue sample required will be explained by your doctor. • Follow any fasting instructions provided by your doctor, if applicable. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with AFB-Smear Examination by Fluorescent Stain – Tissue/Biopsy?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside AFB-Smear Examination by Fluorescent Stain – Tissue/Biopsy include: • Tuberculosis culture: This test helps identify the specific strain of tuberculosis bacteria and determine its drug susceptibility. • GeneXpert MTB/RIF: This molecular test detects the presence of tuberculosis bacteria and identifies drug resistance to rifampicin, a common tuberculosis medication.

faqs.question: What is the AFB-Smear Examination by Fluorescent Stain – Tissue/Biopsy also known as?
faqs.answer: Acid-Fast Bacilli Smear Examination by Fluorescence Microscopy

faqs.question: What is tuberculosis?
faqs.answer: Tuberculosis is a contagious infection caused by the bacteria Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It primarily affects the lungs but can also affect other parts of the body. Common symptoms include persistent cough, weight loss, fever, and night sweats. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial for effective management.

faqs.question: What does Auto Antibody Detection Test measure?
faqs.answer: This test measures the presence of autoantibodies in your blood.

faqs.question: Why is Auto Antibody Detection Test done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose and monitor autoimmune diseases • To assess the severity or activity of an autoimmune disease • To determine the effectiveness of treatment • To rule out other conditions with similar symptoms • To aid in the classification of autoimmune diseases for proper management

faqs.question: When is Auto Antibody Detection Test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend the Auto Antibody Detection Test if you • have symptoms suggesting an autoimmune disease, such as joint pain, rash, fatigue, or digestive issues, • have a family history of autoimmune disease, • show signs of multiple autoimmune diseases, or • need to monitor the progression or recurrence of an autoimmune disease.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Auto Antibody Detection Test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate a specific autoimmune disease, such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Auto Antibody Detection Test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional will insert a needle into a vein in your arm to draw a blood sample. They will send this sample to a laboratory for testing.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Auto Antibody Detection Test?
faqs.answer: • Inform your doctor about any medications or supplements you are taking, as they might interfere with the test results. Also, tell them if you have any specific requirements. • Follow any fasting instructions provided by your doctor, if applicable.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with Auto Antibody Detection Test?
faqs.answer: • Complete blood count (CBC): to evaluate overall health and detect any abnormalities in blood cells • Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C-reactive protein (CRP): to assess inflammation levels • Antinuclear antibody (ANA) test: to screen for autoimmune diseases such as lupus

faqs.question: What is the Auto Antibody Detection Test also known as?
faqs.answer: Autoimmune antibody panel or autoimmune serology tests

faqs.question: What is an autoimmune disease?
faqs.answer: An autoimmune disease occurs when the immune system mistakenly attacks and damages healthy tissues in the body. Examples include rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, multiple sclerosis, and celiac disease. Autoimmune diseases can affect various organs or tissues and cause a range of symptoms.

faqs.answer: This test measures the presence of fungal infections in the stool and identifies the specific type of fungus causing the infection.

faqs.question: Why is the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Stool test done?
faqs.answer: • This test is mainly done to diagnose fungal infections and guide appropriate antifungal treatment. • It also helps assess the effectiveness of ongoing treatment and monitor the progress of the infection.

faqs.question: When is the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Stool test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend this test if you have symptoms such as persistent diarrhea, abdominal pain, or unexplained weight loss, which could be indicative of a fungal infection. faqs.question: What if the results of the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Stool test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results, i.e., results indicating the presence of specific fungi in the stool may point towards a fungal infection.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Stool test?
faqs.answer: During this test, you will be asked to provide a stool sample in a sterile container. The sample will be sent to the laboratory, where it will be cultured on a special medium to promote fungal growth.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Stool test?

faqs.question: What is the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Stool test also known as?

faqs.question: What is a fungal infection?
faqs.answer: A fungal infection is caused by the overgrowth of certain types of fungi. These infections can affect various parts of the body, such as the skin, nails, or internal organs. Common types of fungal infections include candidiasis, ringworm, and aspergillosis.

name: JAK-2 Mutation (CMPD) Exon 12 Mutation Bone Marrow

faqs.question: What does the JAK-2 Mutation (CMPD) Test measure?
faqs.answer: The JAK-2 Mutation (CMPD) Test detects the presence of JAK-2 gene mutations in exon 12 in the bone marrow.

faqs.question: Why is JAK-2 Mutation (CMPD) Test done?
faqs.answer: • To confirm a diagnosis of polycythemia vera when other tests are inconclusive • To identify specific genetic mutations in the JAK-2 gene, which are associated with this condition • To differentiate polycythemia vera from other similar blood disorders

faqs.question: When is JAK-2 Mutation (CMPD) Test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: The JAK-2 Mutation (CMPD) Test may be recommended if you have symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, headaches, or vision problems that suggest polycythemia vera. It is also suggested if other initial screening tests for polycythemia vera are inconclusive or if you have risk factors or a family history of the condition.

faqs.question: What if the results of the JAK-2 Mutation (CMPD) Test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results suggest the presence of mutations associated with polycythemia vera.

faqs.question: What to expect during the JAK-2 Mutation (CMPD) Test?
faqs.answer: During the test, your doctor will draw a bone marrow sample from your hip bone. They will send the sample to the laboratory for testing.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the JAK-2 Mutation (CMPD) Test?
faqs.answer: • Your doctor may ask you to stop taking blood-thinning medications before the test. • Inform your doctor about any other medications or supplements you are taking. Also, tell them if you have any specific requirements. • Follow any additional instructions provided by your doctor regarding fasting or other dietary restrictions before the test.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with JAK-2 Mutation (CMPD) Test?
faqs.answer: • Complete Blood Count (CBC): This test measures various components of your blood, such as red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. • Bone Marrow Biopsy: In this procedure, a small sample of bone marrow is collected for examination under a microscope to evaluate its cellular composition. • Genetic Testing for Other Mutations: Additional genetic tests may be ordered to rule out other potential genetic mutations related to blood disorders.

faqs.question: What is the JAK-2 Mutation (CMPD) Test also known as?
faqs.answer: Jak2 V617F Mutation Test

faqs.question: What is polycythemia vera?
faqs.answer: Polycythemia vera is a rare blood disorder characterised by the overproduction of red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets in the bone marrow. It is usually caused by a mutation in the JAK-2 gene. This condition can lead to an increased risk of blood clots and other complications.

faqs.question: What if the results of the JC-BK Virus DNA Detection Test are abnormal?

faqs.question: What is Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML)?
faqs.answer: PML is a rare but serious disease that affects the central nervous system. It is caused by the JC polyoma virus and can lead to severe neurological symptoms such as vision loss, speech difficulties, and memory problems.

name: Anti Phospholipid Antibody Test
preparation: Heparin should be discontinued for 1 day and oral anticoagulants for 7 days before the test

faqs.question: What does a positive Anti Phospholipid Antibody Test mean?
faqs.answer: A positive result suggests the presence of antibodies linked to Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS) or autoimmune conditions such as Lupus, which may increase your risk of developing blood clots or pregnancy complications.

faqs.question: Can this test confirm Antiphospholipid Syndrome in one go?
faqs.answer: No. A confirmed APS diagnosis requires two positive results taken at least 12 weeks apart along with clinical evidence of clotting or pregnancy-related issues.

faqs.question: Do I need to fast before the Anti Phospholipid Antibody Test?
faqs.answer: Fasting is not required. You can eat and drink normally before the test.

faqs.question: Can medications affect my Anti Phospholipid Antibody Test results?
faqs.answer: Yes. Heparin and oral anticoagulants can interfere with results, so they should be stopped as advised by your doctor before testing.

faqs.question: Are there any risks involved in the test?
faqs.answer: Risks are minimal and similar to any blood draw, including slight bruising or discomfort at the puncture site.

faqs.question: When should the test be repeated?
faqs.answer: If antibodies are detected, your doctor may repeat the test after 12 weeks to confirm persistent positivity, which is essential for APS diagnosis.

name: PRA Plasma Renin Activity
preparation: Clinical history required; dietary and posture instructions must be followed

faqs.question: What does the Plasma Renin Activity test measure?
faqs.answer: It measures the activity of the enzyme renin, which helps control blood pressure and body fluid balance.

faqs.question: Why is posture important for this test?
faqs.answer: Renin levels change depending on whether you are lying down or standing, so posture helps interpret results accurately.

faqs.question: Can I take my usual medicines before the test?
faqs.answer: Some medicines affect renin levels. Inform your doctor before the test so they can guide you appropriately.

faqs.question: Do I need to fast before the test?
faqs.answer: Fasting is not required for the Plasma Renin Activity Test.

faqs.question: How is the sample collected?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional draws about 3 ml of blood from a vein into an EDTA vacutainer for testing.

faqs.question: What can high renin levels indicate?
faqs.answer: High renin levels may suggest adrenal insufficiency, kidney artery narrowing, or certain forms of hypertension.

faqs.question: What do low renin levels mean?
faqs.answer: Low levels may point to conditions like primary hyperaldosteronism or excessive salt and steroid intake.

name: AFB Rapid Culture by Bactec Fx – Bone Marrow

faqs.question: Why is the AFB Rapid Culture by Bactec Fx – Bone Marrow test done?

faqs.question: When is the AFB Rapid Culture by Bactec Fx – Bone Marrow test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended when your doctor suspects an infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Non-tuberculosis bacteria. faqs.question: What if the results of the AFB Rapid Culture by Bactec Fx – Bone Marrow test are abnormal?

faqs.question: What to expect during the AFB Rapid Culture by Bactec Fx – Bone Marrow test?

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the AFB Rapid Culture by Bactec Fx – Bone Marrow test?

Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the AFB Rapid Culture by Bactec Fx – Bone Marrow test?

faqs.question: What is the Metanephrines Free Plasma Test used for?
faqs.answer: It is used to detect rare adrenal or nerve tissue tumours like pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma that produce excess stress hormones.

faqs.question: Is fasting required before the test?
faqs.answer: Yes, you should fast overnight before the test. Only water is allowed.

faqs.question: What should I avoid before the test?
faqs.answer: Avoid bananas, pineapples, chocolates, coffee, ice cream, cereals, vanilla, potatoes, and B-complex vitamins for 48 hours.

faqs.question: Can stress affect the test results?
faqs.answer: Yes, both emotional and physical stress can temporarily raise metanephrine levels.

faqs.question: How is the test performed?
faqs.answer: A small blood sample is taken from your arm after resting for 20–30 minutes, using an EDTA tube for accurate measurement.

faqs.question: What does a high metanephrine level mean?
faqs.answer: It may indicate a hormone-secreting tumour or other conditions causing excess catecholamine activity.

faqs.question: What does the Trisomy (Aneuploidy) Chromosome 13, 18, 21, X,Y by FISH test measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence or absence of abnormal numbers of chromosomes 13, 18, 21, X, and Y in your genetic material.

faqs.question: Why is the Trisomy (Aneuploidy) Chromosome 13, 18, 21, X,Y by FISH test done?
faqs.answer: • Detect genetic conditions like Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18), and Patau syndrome (trisomy 13) • Diagnose sex chromosome abnormalities and aneuploidies like Turner syndrome (monosomy X) and Klinefelter syndrome (XXY) • Assess the risk of certain genetic conditions during pregnancy • Provide valuable information for prenatal counselling and decision-making

faqs.question: When is the Trisomy (Aneuploidy) Chromosome 13, 18, 21, X,Y by FISH test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended when • A pregnant woman wants to assess the risk of genetic abnormalities in the fetus. • A person exhibits physical or developmental abnormalities suggestive of a chromosomal disorder. • There is a family history of genetic disorders or a previous child with a chromosomal abnormality.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Trisomy (Aneuploidy) Chromosome 13, 18, 21, X,Y by FISH test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate the presence of conditions like Down syndrome, Edwards syndrome, Patau syndrome, or sex chromosome aneuploidies. However, abnormal results do not provide a definitive diagnosis and should be discussed with your doctor. Further diagnostic tests like genetic counselling, karyotyping, or microarray testing may be recommended.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Trisomy (Aneuploidy) Chromosome 13, 18, 21, X,Y by FISH test?
faqs.answer: A small amount of amniotic fluid will be collected during a procedure called amniocentesis. The sample will be sent to the laboratory for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Trisomy (Aneuploidy) Chromosome 13, 18, 21, X,Y by FISH test?
faqs.answer: • A detailed clinical history, including an anomaly scan report, must be submitted along with the sample. • A duly signed consent form as per PCPNDT guidelines must be provided. • Follow any instructions provided by your doctor regarding eating and drinking before the procedure. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Trisomy (Aneuploidy) Chromosome 13, 18, 21, X,Y by FISH test?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside the Trisomy (Aneuploidy) Chromosome 13, 18, 21, X,Y by FISH test include: • Detailed ultrasound to assess fetal anatomy • Maternal serum screening tests to assess the risk of chromosomal abnormalities • Genetic counselling to discuss the implications and options based on test results

faqs.question: What is the the Trisomy (Aneuploidy) Chromosome 13, 18, 21, X,Y by FISH test also known as?
faqs.answer: Down syndrome screening, trisomy screening, aneuploidy testing

faqs.question: What is Down syndrome?
faqs.answer: Down syndrome is a genetic disorder caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21. It leads to physical and intellectual disabilities, distinctive facial features, and an increased risk of certain health conditions such as heart defects and thyroid problems.

faqs.question: More Info on Breast Lump histopathology with special stains Test
faqs.answer: Management of breast lump patients varies as the breast presents with different types of non neoplastic to neoplastic lesions. Hence it is important for surgeons to recognize and distinguish benign and premalignant lesions from breast cancer through histopathological examination of biopsy with subsequent immunohistochemistry (IHC) Immunohistochemical markers are often used to guide treatment decisions, to classify breast cancer into subtypes that are biologically distinct and behave differently, and both as prognostic and predictive factors.

name: Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing – Sputum

faqs.question: What does Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing – Sputum measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence of fungal DNA in sputum samples.

faqs.question: Why is Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing – Sputum done?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence of fungal infections in the body by analysing the fungal DNA in sputum samples. Hence, this test is prescribed • To diagnose fungal infections in the respiratory tract. • To identify specific types of fungi causing the infection. • To monitor the effectiveness of antifungal treatment. • To guide clinicians in selecting appropriate antifungal medications. • To differentiate between fungal and bacterial respiratory infections.

faqs.question: When is Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing – Sputum recommended, and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended when you exhibit symptoms such as persistent cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, or fever, which may indicate a respiratory fungal infection. Patients with compromised immune systems, pre-existing lung conditions, or exposure to certain environments may also be advised to take this test.

faqs.question: What if the results of Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing – Sputum are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate the presence of a fungal infection in the respiratory tract. However, further evaluation is necessary to determine the specific type of fungus causing the infection.

faqs.question: What to expect during Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing – Sputum?
faqs.answer: You will be required to provide a sputum sample in a sterile container. The sample will then be sent to the laboratory for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing – Sputum?
faqs.answer: Collect a sputum sample as per the sampling guidelines provided by your healthcare provider. Ensure that the specimen type, site, and relevant clinical history are properly mentioned on the Test Request Form (TRF). Follow any instructions given by your doctor regarding medications or dietary restrictions before the test. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing – Sputum?
faqs.answer: • Fungal culture: A test that helps grow and identify specific types of fungi from samples. • Antifungal susceptibility testing: Determines which antifungal medications are effective against the identified fungal strain. • Chest X-ray or CT scan: Imaging tests to evaluate the extent of lung involvement and identify any complications associated with fungal infections.

faqs.question: What is Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing – Sputum also known as?
faqs.answer: Fungal DNA PCR test, sputum fungal DNA analysis

faqs.question: What is a fungal respiratory infection?
faqs.answer: A fungal respiratory infection is an infection caused by various types of fungi that affect the respiratory system, including the lungs and airways. Symptoms may include coughing, fever, chest pain, and difficulty breathing. Early identification is important for prompt treatment.

faqs.question: What does the Nicotine Metabolite Quantitative Test measure?
faqs.answer: It measures nicotine and its metabolites like cotinine to detect recent tobacco or nicotine exposure.

faqs.question: Is fasting required for this test?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required. You can eat and drink normally before the test.

faqs.question: What do high nicotine metabolite levels mean?
faqs.answer: High levels indicate active nicotine use or exposure from smoking, vaping, or chewing tobacco.

faqs.question: Can this test detect secondhand smoke exposure?
faqs.answer: Yes, it can detect nicotine exposure even from passive smoking environments.

faqs.question: How long can nicotine be detected after smoking?
faqs.answer: Nicotine can be detected for up to 2 days, and cotinine for 3 to 5 days after use.

faqs.question: What does HLA cross-match by Flow cytometry measure?
faqs.answer: HLA cross-match by flow cytometry measures the surface markers present on your immune cells called human leucocyte antigens (HLA) that help identify self-cells from foreign cells.

faqs.question: Why is HLA cross-match by Flow cytometry done?
faqs.answer: • To assess the compatibility of a donor's and recipient's immune system before an organ transplantation • To monitor the effectiveness of immunosuppressive therapy after a transplant • To detect and diagnose autoimmune disorders like diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, celiac disease, etc. • To investigate transfusion reactions, when blood products can trigger an adverse immune response

faqs.question: When is HLA cross-match recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend this test if you • are scheduled for an organ transplant, • have symptoms or a family history of autoimmune disorders, or • experience transfusion reactions or complications after blood transfusions.

faqs.question: What if the results of the HLA cross-match are abnormal?
faqs.answer: The results of the HLA cross-match can be either compatible or incompatible between the donor and recipient. If it's incompatible, it may result in the rejection of an organ transplant or immune-mediated complications.

faqs.question: What to expect during the HLA cross-match?
faqs.answer: • Blood samples will be collected from both the recipient and donor. • The samples will be processed in the laboratory through flow cytometry.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the HLA cross-match?
faqs.answer: • Avoid medications that can interfere with your test results. • Inform your doctor if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with HLA cross-match?
faqs.answer: • Complete Blood Count (CBC) • Serum creatinine levels • Liver function tests • Additional HLA testing, such as HLA typing

faqs.question: What is the HLA cross-match by Flow cytometry also known as?
faqs.answer: Histocompatibility testing or HLA compatibility testing

faqs.question: What is organ transplantation?
faqs.answer: Organ transplantation is a surgical procedure where an organ from one person (donor) is transplanted into another person's (recipient) body to replace a damaged or diseased organ. Common examples include liver, kidney, heart, lungs or pancreas transplants.
