faqs.question: What does AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Levofloxacin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex measure?
faqs.answer: This test measures the drug susceptibility of the MTb complex (Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex) to levofloxacin, an antibiotic used in the treatment of tuberculosis (TB).

faqs.question: Why is AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Levofloxacin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex done?
faqs.answer: • This test helps determine if the bacteria causing the tuberculosis infection are responsive or resistant to levofloxacin. • To guide the selection of antibiotics for treating TB based on drug susceptibility. • To monitor the effectiveness of ongoing TB treatment. • To identify drug-resistant strains of the MTb complex. • To prevent the development and spread of drug-resistant TB strains.

faqs.question: When is AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Levofloxacin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended for • Patients diagnosed with TB to determine their specific drug susceptibility profile. • Patients with a history of non-response or relapse during TB treatment. • Individuals suspected of having drug-resistant TB due to close contact with a known case. • Patients who have completed initial treatment for TB but are experiencing persistent symptoms.

faqs.question: What if the results of AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Levofloxacin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may suggest resistance to levofloxacin, requiring alternative antibiotics or modified treatment regimens.

faqs.question: What to expect during AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Levofloxacin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex?
faqs.answer: During the collection process, a sputum or other appropriate sample will be collected for testing.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Levofloxacin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex?
faqs.answer: Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Levofloxacin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex?
faqs.answer: • TB culture and sensitivity testing to assess drug susceptibility against other antibiotics • Chest X-ray to evaluate the extent of lung involvement in TB

faqs.question: What is AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Levofloxacin Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex also known as?
faqs.answer: MTb complex levofloxacin susceptibility testing, MTb complex drug sensitivity testing for levofloxacin

faqs.question: What is tuberculosis (TB)?
faqs.answer: Tuberculosis, commonly known as TB, is an infectious disease caused by the bacteria Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It primarily affects the lungs but can also impact other organs. TB is usually spread through the air when an infected individual coughs or sneezes. It can cause symptoms such as persistent cough, weight loss, fatigue, and night sweats.

faqs.question: What does Cytopathology – Expert Opinion measure?
faqs.answer: Cytopathology – Expert Opinion is a second opinion from experts that conduct a thorough review and analysis, potentially offering further insights, confirming diagnoses, or suggesting alternative interpretations.

faqs.question: Why is Cytopathology – Expert Opinion done?
faqs.answer: Cytopathology – Expert Opinion is done for several reasons, including: • Diagnosing diseases and conditions by analysing cellular changes and determining their severity • Assessing the effectiveness of ongoing treatments • Monitoring disease progression and recurrence • Providing expert opinions for complex cases or for second opinions

faqs.question: When is Cytopathology – Expert Opinion recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Cytopathology – Expert Opinion is recommended in various situations, including: • When a specific diagnosis could not be made with routine tests • When there is a need for an expert opinion in complex cases or for a second opinion • To assess treatment effectiveness and monitor disease progression

faqs.question: What if the results of Cytopathology – Expert Opinion are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate the presence of underlying diseases or conditions. However, abnormal results do not necessarily mean a serious or life-threatening condition. It is important to discuss the results with your doctor, who will interpret them in the context of your medical history, other tests, and clinical findings.

faqs.question: What to expect during Cytopathology – Expert Opinion?
faqs.answer: During this test: • You will need to provide stained or unstained slides along with the original cytopathology report. • Relevant clinical and radiological details should also be provided. • The samples will be analysed by expert pathologists who will provide an opinion based on the findings.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before Cytopathology – Expert Opinion?
faqs.answer: To prepare for Cytopathology – Expert Opinion: • Collect and provide the required stained or unstained slides. • Include the original cytopathology report. • Provide relevant clinical and radiological details. • Follow any specific instructions from your doctor regarding fasting or medication restrictions. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with Cytopathology – Expert Opinion?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside Cytopathology – Expert Opinion include: • Histopathology: This involves examining tissue samples under a microscope to diagnose diseases. • Molecular Testing: It helps identify genetic mutations or specific markers associated with certain diseases. • Immunohistochemistry: This test uses specific antibodies to detect proteins in tissues and can aid in diagnosis and prognosis.

faqs.question: What is Cytopathology – Expert Opinion also known as?
faqs.answer: Expert pathological analysis of cell samples

faqs.question: What is cytopathology used for?
faqs.answer: Cytopathology can be used to diagnose various diseases and conditions, such as cancer, infections, autoimmune disorders, inflammatory conditions, and hormonal disorders. It helps in identifying specific cell abnormalities and provides important information for accurate diagnosis and treatment planning.

name: Candida Albicans Ab By Indirect Haemagglutination - Serum

faqs.question: What does the Candida Albicans Test measure?
faqs.answer: The Candida Albicans Test detects the presence of Candida albicans in your body.

faqs.question: Why is the Candida Albicans Test done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose Candida albicans infections • To monitor the effectiveness of treatment for Candida Albican infections • To assess the risk of developing Candida-related complications in individuals with suppressed immune systems

faqs.question: When is the Candida Albicans Test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend the Candida Albicans Test if you have • symptoms suggestive of a Candida Albican infection, such as oral thrush, vaginal yeast infection, or skin rashes • a weakened immune system due to conditions like HIV/AIDS, cancer, or organ transplantation • prolonged use of antibiotics or corticosteroids • uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, or • frequent episodes of fungal infections.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Candida Albicans Test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: If the results are abnormal (positive), it suggests the presence of an active infection or colonisation by Candida albicans.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Candida Albicans Test?
faqs.answer: During the test, a blood sample is collected from a vein in your arm using a needle. The sample is then sent to the laboratory for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Candida Albicans Test?
faqs.answer: Inform your doctor about any medications you are taking, including over-the-counter drugs, as they may affect the test results. Also, tell them if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Candida Albicans Test?
faqs.answer: • Fungal Culture: This test helps identify the type of fungus causing the infection and determine its susceptibility to antifungal medications. • Antifungal Sensitivity Testing: It helps guide appropriate treatment by determining which antifungal medications are effective against the specific strain of Candida albicans.

faqs.question: What is the Candida Albicans Test also known as?
faqs.answer: Candida Serology Test or Anti-Candida Antibody Test

faqs.question: What is Candidiasis?
faqs.answer: Candidiasis is an infection caused by Candida species, most commonly Candida albicans. It can affect various parts of the body, including the mouth (oral thrush), genital area (vaginal yeast infection), skin, and nails.

name: Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Tissue

faqs.question: What does the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Tissue test measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence of fungal infections by identifying the specific type of fungus in a tissue sample.

faqs.question: Why is the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Tissue test done?
faqs.answer: • This test helps determine the causative agent responsible for the fungal infection, which is crucial for guiding appropriate antifungal therapy. • It is also used to monitor the effectiveness of ongoing antifungal therapy. • Identifying the specific type of fungus causing the infection • Assessing the severity and extent of fungal infections • Evaluating the risk of complications associated with fungal infections • Guiding infection control measures in healthcare settings

faqs.question: When is the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Tissue test recommended, and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend this test if you have • Suspected or confirmed fungal infections, such as candidiasis, aspergillosis, or mucormycosis. • Persistent or recurrent symptoms suggestive of a fungal infection. • Immunosuppression or other conditions that increase the risk of fungal infections. • Infections that have not responded to initial antifungal treatment. • Complications related to fungal infections, such as tissue invasion or organ involvement.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Tissue test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results indicate that a growth of fungus has been observed, indicating a fungal infection.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Tissue test?
faqs.answer: During this test, a tissue sample will be collected from the affected site using a sterile leak-proof container. The sample will be sent to the laboratory for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Tissue test?
faqs.answer: • Follow any specific instructions provided by your doctor regarding fasting or medication restrictions.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Tissue test?
faqs.answer: • Blood tests to assess the severity of infection and monitor response to treatment • Imaging studies such as X-rays or CT scans, to evaluate the extent and spread of the infection • Biopsy to obtain a tissue sample for further analysis, if necessary

faqs.question: What is the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Tissue test also known as?
faqs.answer: Fungal Culture and Identification by Matrix-Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation Time-of-Flight Mass Spectrometry (MALDITOF) Tissue

faqs.question: What is the most probable indicated disease or health condition diagnosed after the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Tissue test?
faqs.answer: Fungal infections, such as candidiasis, aspergillosis, or mucormycosis, are the most probable conditions diagnosed. This test provides essential information for diagnosing these infections accurately and guiding appropriate treatment.

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the PPBS test?
faqs.answer: The blood sample must be collected exactly 2 hours after you start eating your meal. Accurate timing is crucial for reliable results, so it's important to note when you begin eating and ensure the blood draw occurs precisely at the 2-hour mark.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the PPBS test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required for the PPBS test. Unlike fasting blood sugar tests, the PPBS test specifically requires you to eat a normal meal before the blood sample is taken to evaluate your body's response to food.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my PPBS test results?
faqs.answer: Yes, dehydration can concentrate your blood and lead to falsely high glucose readings. Stay well-hydrated before your test for accurate results and comfort.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the PPBS test?
faqs.answer: Eat a regular meal with adequate carbohydrates like rice or bread. Inform your doctor about all medications, especially diabetes medicines, for proper guidance.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the PPBS test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional cleans your arm with an antiseptic wipe, then inserts a sterile needle into a vein to draw blood into a special fluoride tube. The entire process takes less than five minutes and causes minimal discomfort.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: The PPBS test carries minimal health risks similar to any blood draw. You may experience slight pain, bruising at the needle site, or feel lightheaded. Serious complications like infection are extremely rare.

faqs.question: What level of PPBS test is normal?
faqs.answer: Normal PPBS levels are less than 140 mg/dL. Levels between 140-199 mg/dL indicate impaired glucose tolerance (prediabetes), while levels of 200 mg/dL or higher on more than one occasion suggest diabetes mellitus according to American Diabetes Association guidelines.

faqs.question: What is the PPBS test also known as?
faqs.answer: The PPBS test is also known as the Post Prandial Blood Sugar Test, Glucose Post Prandial Test, 2-hour post-prandial glucose test, 2-hour PG test, or simply the post-meal blood sugar test.

faqs.question: Why is RNP-Sm Antibody Serum test done?
faqs.answer: RNP-Sm test is done to diagnose Sharp syndrome. Patients can have as signs and symptoms of a combination of disorders — primarily lupus, scleroderma, polymyositis, and Sjogren's syndrome characterized by numbness and puffiness of fingers, muscle and joint pain, fatigue and fever, rash , skin lesions, shortness of breath, chest pain, dry eyes etc

faqs.question: What does it measure?
faqs.answer: The blood test measures the presence of RNA-Sm antibodies by ELISA technique.

faqs.question: What to expect during the test?
faqs.answer: The blood sample is taken from a vein in your arm, using a small needle. After the needle is inserted, a small amount of blood will be collected into a test tube or vial. You may feel a little sting when the needle goes in or out. This usually takes less than five minutes.

faqs.question: What if results are Present/ Absent?
faqs.answer: Positive RNP-Sm antibodies in the absence of other ANA antibodies may be highly suggestive of Mixed connective tissue disorders. Results need to be correlated with clinical symptoms. Negative result does not rule out connective tissue disease as certain cases may show negative result.

name: AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Isoniazid Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex

faqs.question: What does AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Isoniazid Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex measure?
faqs.answer: This test determines the drug susceptibility of the MTb complex to isoniazid.

faqs.question: Why is AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Isoniazid Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex done?
faqs.answer: • To determine if the bacteria causing TB are resistant or sensitive to isoniazid. • To guide doctors in prescribing appropriate treatment plans for patients with TB. • To minimise the risk of drug resistance by selecting effective medications. • To monitor and evaluate treatment effectiveness and make necessary adjustments.

faqs.question: When is AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Isoniazid Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test may be recommended if you • Have been diagnosed with TB and need to determine drug susceptibility. • Require a change in your TB medication due to treatment failure or drug resistance. • Are at high risk of developing drug-resistant TB. • Have been exposed to someone with drug-resistant TB. • Have recurrent or persistent symptoms of TB despite receiving treatment.

faqs.question: What if the results of the AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Isoniazid Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results suggest that the bacteria causing TB may be resistant to isoniazid.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Isoniazid Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex?
faqs.answer: Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Isoniazid Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside this test include: • AFB smear microscopy: This test helps identify the presence of acid-fast bacilli (AFB) in sputum or other specimens. • Xpert MTB/RIF assay: This molecular test detects the presence of TB bacteria and checks for rifampicin resistance.

faqs.question: What is the AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Isoniazid Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex also known as?
faqs.answer: Isoniazid susceptibility test for the MTb complex

faqs.question: What is tuberculosis (TB)?
faqs.answer: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease caused by the bacteria Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It primarily affects the lungs but can also affect other parts of the body. TB spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Common symptoms include persistent cough, weight loss, fatigue, and night sweats. Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment are crucial for managing TB effectively.

name: Culture And Identification, Anaerobic Bacteria - High Vagina Discharge

faqs.question: What does Culture and Identification test - Anaerobic bacteria - Vagina Discharge measure?
faqs.answer: This test identifies the presence of anaerobic bacteria in vaginal discharge.

faqs.question: Why is Culture and Identification test - Anaerobic bacteria - Vagina Discharge done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose anaerobic bacterial infections in the vagina • To identify the specific bacteria causing the infection • To monitor the effectiveness of treatment and prevent recurrent infections

faqs.question: When is Culture and Identification test - Anaerobic bacteria - Vagina Discharge recommended, and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend this test if you have symptoms such as abnormal vaginal discharge, itching, or odour. It is particularly useful for women with recurrent vaginal infections or those who do not respond well to standard treatments.

faqs.question: What if the results of Culture and Identification test - Anaerobic bacteria - Vagina Discharge are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Usually, the presence of anaerobic bacteria indicates an infection in the vagina.

faqs.question: What to expect during Culture and Identification test - Anaerobic bacteria - Vagina Discharge?
faqs.answer: You will need to provide a sample of vaginal discharge in a sterile, leak-proof container. The laboratory will use advanced techniques like Vitek or MALDITOF to identify the anaerobic bacteria present in the sample.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before Culture and Identification test - Anaerobic bacteria - Vagina Discharge?
faqs.answer: • Inform your doctor about any ongoing medications or allergies. Also, tell them if you have any specific requirements. • Avoid using vaginal creams, douches, or other products at least 24 hours before the test.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with Culture and Identification test - Anaerobic bacteria - Vagina Discharge?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may order additional tests for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or other types of bacterial infections.

faqs.question: What is Culture and Identification test - Anaerobic bacteria - Vagina Discharge also known as?
faqs.answer: Anaerobic Bacterial Culture and Identification of Vaginal Discharge

faqs.question: What is anaerobic bacterial vaginosis?
faqs.answer: Anaerobic bacterial vaginosis is a condition characterised by an overgrowth of anaerobic bacteria in the vagina. It can cause symptoms such as abnormal vaginal discharge, itching, and odour.

name: Sputum Culture Test (Culture & Sensitivity – Aerobic Bacteria, Sputum
preparation: Collect deep cough sputum in a sterile leak-proof container, preferably early morning

faqs.question: What is a Sputum Culture Test used for?
faqs.answer: It detects bacteria causing lung infections and helps select effective antibiotics for treatment.

faqs.question: How is sputum collected for this test?
faqs.answer: You rinse your mouth, then cough deeply to produce mucus from your lungs into a sterile container.

faqs.question: How long does the Sputum Culture Test take?
faqs.answer: The test usually takes 4 days to allow bacterial growth and antibiotic sensitivity analysis.

faqs.question: What does a positive Sputum Culture Test mean?
faqs.answer: It means bacteria are present in your lungs, suggesting a bacterial infection such as pneumonia or bronchitis.

faqs.question: Can antibiotics affect the test results?
faqs.answer: Yes, taking antibiotics before the test may prevent bacterial growth and affect accuracy.

faqs.question: Is fasting required for the Sputum Culture Test?
faqs.answer: Fasting is not required. You can have food and water as usual.

faqs.question: What if my sputum culture shows no bacterial growth?
faqs.answer: No growth usually means there is no bacterial infection, but your doctor may recommend further tests if symptoms persist.

name: LDH Lactate Dehydrogenase Serum Test
preparation: 3 ml of serum for a single test

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the LDH test?
faqs.answer: There is no specific best time to take an LDH test. You can have this test done at any time of the day as instructed by your doctor, since it doesn't require fasting or special timing considerations.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the LDH test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is generally not required for a standalone LDH test. However, if your LDH test is part of a larger panel requiring fasting, you'll need to follow those specific instructions, typically 8-12 hours.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my LDH test results?
faqs.answer: Yes, severe dehydration can lead to a blood concentration, which may falsely elevate LDH levels. It's advisable to stay well-hydrated before your test unless your doctor instructs otherwise for specific medical reasons.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the LDH test?
faqs.answer: No special diet is needed before an LDH test. However, inform your doctor about all medications, vitamins, and supplements you're taking, as certain drugs like statins and aspirin can affect LDH levels.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the LDH test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional cleans your arm, ties an elastic band around your upper arm, inserts a sterile needle into a vein, collects the blood sample, removes the needle, and applies a bandage.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: The risks are minimal and similar to any standard blood draw. You may experience slight pain, minor bruising, light-headedness, or, in very rare cases, infection at the needle site.

faqs.question: What level of LDH test is normal?
faqs.answer: Normal LDH levels typically range from 0 to 250 U/L for adults.

faqs.question: What is the LDH test also known as?
faqs.answer: The LDH test is also known as the Lactate Dehydrogenase test or the Lactic Acid Dehydrogenase test. These are alternative names for the same diagnostic procedure that measures this important enzyme.

faqs.question: What does Fibroblast Growth Factor 23, Plasma measure?
faqs.answer: The test measures the Fibroblast Growth Factor 23 levels in the blood plasma.

faqs.question: Why is Fibroblast Growth Factor 23, Plasma Test Done?
faqs.answer: • FG23 test is done to monitor the progression of chronic kidney disease by monitoring the renal clearance status. • The test aids the diagnosis of hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets and diagnosis and follow-up of tumor-induced osteomalacia.

faqs.question: Who Should Get Fibroblast Growth Factor 23, Plasma Test Done?
faqs.answer: • CKD patients at risk for altered phosphorus metabolism due to malfunctioning of the kidneys. • Patients with bone disorders like hereditary rickets which may affect the phosphorus and vitamin D metabolism. • The test may also be advised for patients with certain types of bone tumors.

faqs.question: What to expect during Fibroblast Growth Factor 23, Plasma test?
faqs.answer: The test requires a blood plasma sample. A tourniquet (elastic) band is placed tightly on the upper arm. The patient is then asked to make a fist. This helps in the build-up of blood filling the veins. The skin is disinfected before needle insertion and the blood sample is collected in vacutainer.

faqs.question: Are any preparations required for Fibroblast Growth Factor 23, Plasma test?
faqs.answer: No special precautions.

faqs.question: What if results are High/ Low?
faqs.answer: Elevated levels are associated with increased adverse outcome and is a predictor of mortality in CKD. Increased levels are seen in Autosomal Dominant Hypophosphatemic Rickets, X-linked Hypophosphatemia Rickets, Fibrous Dysplasia and tumor induced osteomalacia.

name: ALK (D5F3) IHC reflex to FISH for NSCLC
Leukemia panel by FISH - CLL, Leukemic Blood
Fungal Culture And Identification Test By MALDITOF (Vitek MS) - Bone Marrow

faqs.question: What does the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - Bone Marrow measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence of fungal infection in the bone marrow.

faqs.question: Why is the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - Bone Marrow done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose fungal infections, specifically in the bone marrow • To determine the appropriate antifungal treatment for patients with suspected or confirmed fungal infections

faqs.question: When is the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - Bone Marrow recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended when there are symptoms suggestive of fungal infection, such as persistent fever, fatigue, unexplained weight loss, or signs of bone marrow involvement. Patients with weakened immune systems or those who have received recent organ transplants may also undergo this test.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - Bone Marrow are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results from this test may indicate the presence of a fungal infection in the bone marrow.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - Bone Marrow?
faqs.answer: During this test, a small sample of bone marrow will be collected using a specialised bottle or sodium heparin. The sample will be sent to the laboratory for analysis using automated MALDITOF (Vitek MS).

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - Bone Marrow?
faqs.answer: • Provide accurate clinical history, including information about your symptoms, medical conditions, and any recent antibiotic or antifungal treatments. • Inform your doctor if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - Bone Marrow?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - Bone Marrow include blood tests and other microbiological tests such as bacterial cultures or viral PCR tests to rule out other possible infections.

faqs.question: What is the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - Bone Marrow also known as?
faqs.answer: Fungal culture of bone marrow or mycology culture of bone marrow

faqs.question: What is a fungal infection in bone marrow?
faqs.answer: A fungal infection in the bone marrow occurs when fungi invade the bone marrow tissue. This can result in various symptoms, depending on the type of fungus involved.

faqs.question: What are the different types of HIV tests?
faqs.answer: There are three main types: antigen/antibody combination tests (like HIV-Duo), antibody-only tests, and nucleic acid tests. The HIV-Duo test is highly recommended, as it detects both antigens and antibodies, providing earlier and more accurate results than other tests.

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the HIV test?
faqs.answer: For the HIV-Duo test, the optimal time is 18-45 days after potential exposure. This allows sufficient time for both P24 antigens and antibodies to develop to detectable levels, ensuring accurate results while minimising the window period.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the HIV test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required for HIV testing. You can eat and drink normally before the test. The presence of HIV antigens and antibodies in your blood is not affected by food intake or fasting status.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my HIV test results?
faqs.answer: Dehydration does not affect the accuracy of HIV test results for detecting antigens or antibodies. However, severe dehydration may make blood collection more difficult for the technician, so staying adequately hydrated is recommended for comfort during the procedure.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the HIV test
faqs.answer: No special dietary preparation is needed. Continue taking your regular medications, but inform your doctor about all medicines, especially HIV prevention drugs like PrEP or PEP, as these may potentially affect test interpretation and timing.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the HIV test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional cleans your arm with an antiseptic, ties an elastic band around your upper arm, inserts a small needle into your vein, and collects blood in a special tube. The entire procedure takes less than five minutes.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: Risks are minimal and similar to any routine blood test. You may experience slight pain, minor bruising at the needle site, or occasional dizziness. Serious complications, like infection, are extremely rare when proper protocols are followed.

faqs.question: What level of HIV test is normal?
faqs.answer: HIV test results are reported as either non-reactive (normal) with values less than 1.0 S/CO or reactive (preliminary positive) with values of 1.0 S/CO or higher. A non-reactive result means no HIV infection was detected.

faqs.question: What is an HIV test also known as?
faqs.answer: The HIV-Duo test is also called the HIV 4th Generation Test, the HIV Antigen/Antibody Combination Test, or the HIV-1/2 Ab & p24 Ag Test. All these names refer to the same advanced screening method that detects both antigens and antibodies.

faqs.question: Is the HIV test accurate?
faqs.answer: Yes, modern HIV tests, including the HIV-Duo, are extremely accurate, with over 99% reliability when performed correctly after the window period. All reactive screening results require confirmatory testing to establish a definitive diagnosis, ensuring maximum accuracy.

faqs.question: How early can HIV be detected?
faqs.answer: The HIV-Duo test can typically detect HIV infection as early as 18 days after exposure, though it may take up to 45 days for definitive results. This makes it one of the earliest detection methods available for HIV screening.

name: Calcitonin Serum Test
preparation: Avoid high-dose biotin supplements (more than 5 mg/day) for at least 8 hours before blood collection

faqs.question: What does the Calcitonin Test measure?
faqs.answer: It measures the level of calcitonin hormone in your blood, produced by thyroid C-cells.

faqs.question: Why is this test done?
faqs.answer: It helps diagnose and monitor medullary thyroid carcinoma and C-cell hyperplasia

faqs.question: Do I need to fast before the test?
faqs.answer: Fasting is not required.

faqs.question: Can supplements affect my results?
faqs.answer: Yes, high doses of biotin can interfere with results; stop taking them 8 hours before your test.

faqs.question: What are normal calcitonin levels?
faqs.answer: Typically below 10.2 pg/mL, though normal ranges may vary slightly by lab.

faqs.question: What does a high calcitonin level mean?
faqs.answer: It may suggest medullary thyroid carcinoma, C-cell hyperplasia, or other conditions such as chronic liver disease.

faqs.question: How is the test performed?
faqs.answer: A simple blood sample is drawn from a vein in your arm and analysed using ECLIA.

faqs.question: When will I get my report?
faqs.answer: Reports are usually ready within 8 hours after the sample reaches the lab.

name: JC DNA Detection by Real-time PCR - CSF

faqs.question: What does JC DNA Detection by Real-time PCR - CSF measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence of JC polyomavirus in cerebrospinal fluid obtained through lumbar puncture.

faqs.question: Why is JC DNA Detection by Real-time PCR - CSF done?
faqs.answer: • To detect the JC polyomavirus • To monitor the effectiveness of treatment • To evaluate patients with weakened immune systems who are at risk of developing this condition

faqs.question: When is the JC DNA Detection test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: • This test is recommended for people suspected to have progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. • It is also suggested for patients with weakened immune systems due to conditions such as HIV/AIDS, haematological malignancies, and organ transplants. • Patients undergoing immunosuppressive therapies should also take this test.

faqs.question: What if the results of the JC DNA Detection test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Positive results indicate the presence of the virus and thus the risk of developing progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.

faqs.question: What to expect during the JC DNA Detection test?
faqs.answer: During the test, a small sample of cerebrospinal fluid is obtained through a lumbar puncture. The sample is then sent to a laboratory for testing.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the JC DNA Detection test?
faqs.answer: • Inform your doctor about any medications you are taking, especially those that affect your immune system. You may have to stop taking certain medications before the test. Your doctor may also advise you to fast for a few hours before the test. • Avoid blood-thinning medications, such as aspirin and ibuprofen, for at least 48 hours before the test. • Inform your doctor if you have any allergies or medical conditions or if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the JC DNA Detection test?
faqs.answer: • Serological tests: Blood tests to detect other viral infections • Examination of blood samples: To assess the immune status of immunocompromised patients

faqs.question: What is JC DNA Detection by Real-time PCR - CSF also known as?
faqs.answer: Real-time PCR for JC virus, JC virus DNA in CSF, or JC virus detection by PCR

faqs.question: What is progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML)?
faqs.answer: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a rare but serious brain infection caused by the JC virus. It affects people with weakened immune systems and patients undergoing immunosuppressive therapies. It can lead to severe neurological problems, including confusion, memory loss, and motor deficits.

faqs.question: What does the Cyclosporine – By LCMS, Blood test measure?
faqs.answer: This test measures the concentration of cyclosporine drug in your blood.

faqs.question: Why is the Cyclosporine – By LCMS, Blood test done?
faqs.answer: Cyclosporine is a drug to prevent organ rejection in people who have received a liver, kidney, or heart transplant. Hence, this test is primarily done to monitor the level of cyclosporine in the blood for transplant recipients. It is also done to • Determine if the body is receiving enough medication to prevent organ rejection after a transplant and assess if the dosage is optimal or needs adjustment. • Evaluate the effectiveness of treatment. • Determine the cause of adverse effects. • Ensure compliance with medication guidelines.

faqs.question: When is the Cyclosporine – By LCMS, Blood test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend this test if you have undergone a liver, kidney, or heart transplant. Additionally, individuals who experience symptoms of organ rejection or potential side effects of cyclosporine may be advised to undergo this test. It is also performed during routine follow-up visits to ensure medication effectiveness.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Cyclosporine – By LCMS, Blood test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate suboptimal drug levels, which can lead to organ rejection or increased risk of side effects. However, abnormal results do not necessarily indicate immediate danger and should be discussed with your doctor for appropriate action.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Cyclosporine – By LCMS, Blood test?
faqs.answer: The test involves a simple blood draw. A healthcare professional will collect a small sample of your blood using a needle. The procedure is quick and usually causes only minor discomfort. After the sample is collected, it will be sent to the laboratory for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Cyclosporine – By LCMS, Blood test?
faqs.answer: To prepare for this test: • Ensure you provide information about the drug dose taken, time of sample collection (peak or trough levels), and clinical history. • Follow any specific dietary or medication restrictions provided by your doctor. • It is important to discuss any concerns or questions about the test with your healthcare provider. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Cyclosporine – By LCMS, Blood test?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside the Cyclosporine – By LCMS, Blood test include: • Liver and kidney function tests: These tests help assess how well your transplanted organ is functioning. • Complete blood count (CBC): This test provides information about your overall health and can detect any abnormalities. • Renal function tests: These tests evaluate kidney function and monitor for potential complications.

faqs.question: What is the Cyclosporine – By LCMS, Blood test also known as?
faqs.answer: Cyclosporine level test, cyclosporine concentration measurement

faqs.question: What is organ rejection after transplantation?
faqs.answer: Organ rejection occurs when the immune system identifies a transplanted organ as foreign and attacks it. This can happen after a liver, kidney, or heart transplant. Monitoring cyclosporine levels with the Cyclosporine – By LCMS, Blood test helps prevent organ rejection and ensure the success of the transplant.

name: AFB Drug Susceptibility Panel Comprehensive Panel 13 Drugs By MGIT - Pure Culture

preparation: Avoid sexual intercourse, douching, tampons, and vaginal medications for 48 hours before the test.

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the ALP Test?
faqs.answer: The ALP test can be done at any time of day since no fasting is required. Follow any specific instructions provided by your doctor.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the ALP Test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, overnight fasting is not mandatory for the ALP test. You can eat and drink normally before the test, making it convenient to schedule at any time that suits you.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my ALP Test results?
faqs.answer: Yes, dehydration can potentially affect ALP test results by concentrating blood substances, which may lead to falsely elevated readings. It's recommended to stay well-hydrated before your blood test for accurate results.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the ALP Test?
faqs.answer: No special diet preparation is needed for the ALP test. However, inform your doctor about all medications, vitamins, and supplements you're taking, as some may affect ALP levels and require temporary adjustment.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the ALP Test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional cleans your arm, ties an elastic band around your upper arm, inserts a small needle into the vein, and collects blood into a vial. The entire process takes only minutes.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: The risks are minimal and similar to any standard blood test. You might experience slight pain during blood draw, minor bruising at the needle site, or feel faint. Serious complications are very rare.

faqs.question: What level of ALP Test is normal?
faqs.answer: The normal range for ALP is 40-129 U/L for adults. However, children and pregnant women naturally have higher levels due to bone growth and development.

faqs.question: What is ALP Test also known as?
faqs.answer: The ALP test is also known by several names including ALK Phos, Alk Phos, ALP, and ALKP.

name: FISH for Aneuploidy in POC - Chromosomes - 13,16,18, 21, 22, X and Y Test

faqs.question: Why take FISH for Aneuploidy in POC - Chromosomes - 13,16,18, 21, 22, X and Y Test?
faqs.answer: Helps understand genetic results better.

faqs.question: Is this test for you?
faqs.answer: This test is done on POC (abortous tissue) samples to evaluate cause (genetic) of miscarriage.

faqs.question: More Info on FISH for Aneuploidy in POC - Chromosomes - 13,16,18, 21, 22, X and Y Test
faqs.answer: Helps understand genetic results better, asses recurrence risk and plan for future pregnancies and preventive measures.

name: Dengue IgM Test
preparation: Specimen type, site, clinical history and clinician contact details required

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the Dengue Antibody IgM Test?
faqs.answer: The test is usually more useful from the 5th day of fever onwards. Testing too early may give a negative result even if dengue is present.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the Dengue Antibody IgM Test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, overnight fasting is not required. You can eat and drink normally before the test.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my Dengue Antibody IgM Test results?
faqs.answer: Mild dehydration is unlikely to directly affect Dengue IgM antibody detection, but normal hydration can make blood collection easier and more comfortable.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the Dengue Antibody IgM Test?
faqs.answer: No special diet is needed. Inform your doctor about all medicines you take and avoid self-medication for fever or pain unless advised by your doctor.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the Dengue Antibody IgM Test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional ties a tourniquet around your arm, cleans the puncture site, inserts a sterile needle into a vein and collects about 3 ml of blood in a gel vacutainer.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: The risks are minimal and similar to any routine blood test. You may feel slight pain, mild bruising or temporary swelling at the needle site. Rarely, some people may feel dizzy.

faqs.question: What level of Dengue Antibody IgM Test is normal?
faqs.answer: A negative result, less than 1 ratio, is considered within the negative reference range. A result greater than or equal to 1 ratio is interpreted as positive and should be reviewed by your doctor.

name: Alpha Glucosidase GSD II Blood Test

preparation: Avoid high-dose biotin supplements (>5 mg/day) for at least 8 hours before the test

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the Thyroid Panel-4?
faqs.answer: The test can be taken at any time of the day, but morning collection is often preferred for consistency.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the Thyroid Panel-4, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No fasting is required. You can eat and drink normally before your test.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my Thyroid Panel-4 results?
faqs.answer: Severe dehydration may affect blood concentration but doesn’t significantly impact thyroid hormone levels. It’s best to stay well hydrated.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the Thyroid Panel-4?
faqs.answer: You don’t need any special diet. Inform your doctor about thyroid or biotin supplements, as they may affect results.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the Thyroid Panel-4?
faqs.answer: A small amount of blood is collected from your arm using a sterile needle. The process takes only a few minutes.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: Minimal risks include mild pain or bruising at the needle site, which usually resolve quickly.

faqs.question: What level of thyroid hormones is considered normal?
faqs.answer: FT4: 0.93–1.7 ng/dL, TSH: 0.54–5.3 µIU/mL. Reference ranges may slightly vary by laboratory.

name: HCV RNA Viral Load Test by TaqMan RT PCR - serum or plasma

faqs.question: What does an HCV Viral Load Test detect?
faqs.answer: It measures the amount of Hepatitis C virus RNA in your blood to confirm an active infection and monitor treatment effectiveness.

faqs.question: Do I need to fast before the HCV Viral Load Test?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not needed before the test

faqs.question: What does a high HCV viral load mean?
faqs.answer: A high viral load indicates active replication of the virus and a higher risk of liver damage.

faqs.question: What does “Target Not Detected” mean?
faqs.answer: It means that HCV RNA is not found in your blood sample, suggesting successful treatment or remission.

faqs.question: How long does it take to receive the report?
faqs.answer: Reports are generally ready on the same day, by 11:00 PM.

faqs.question: How often should I repeat the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend repeat testing during treatment or follow-up to monitor progress.

faqs.question: What if my result is “Below 15 IU/mL”?
faqs.answer: It means the virus is present at a very low level that cannot be accurately measured. Your doctor will decide if further monitoring is needed.

faqs.question: Is a “Target Not Detected” result the same as being HCV negative?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily; it means the virus is below detection limits but does not always confirm complete elimination.

faqs.question: Is this test part of a routine health check-up?
faqs.answer: The HCV Viral Load Test is primarily done for diagnosis and monitoring of Hepatitis C, not as a preventive screening.

faqs.question: Why take test_name?

faqs.question: Is this test for you?
faqs.answer: This is the Cholesterol-Total test

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the cholesterol test?
faqs.answer: The best time is in the morning, especially after completing the required 12 - 14-hour fasting period. A morning appointment helps you complete the overnight fasting period comfortably while ensuring accurate results.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the cholesterol test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: Yes, fasting for 12-14 hours is required for accurate results. During this period, you can only drink water. Fasting ensures triglyceride levels aren't affected by recent food intake.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my cholesterol test results?
faqs.answer: Yes, dehydration can make your blood more concentrated, potentially causing falsely elevated cholesterol levels. Stay well-hydrated by drinking water even during the fasting period.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the cholesterol test?
faqs.answer: Maintain your normal diet for several days before testing. Fast for 12-14 hours before the test. Continue prescribed medications unless advised otherwise by your doctor.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the cholesterol test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional cleans your arm, ties a tourniquet, inserts a sterile needle into a vein, collects blood into a vial, then removes the needle and applies a bandage. The procedure is quick and generally painless.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: The cholesterol test is very safe with minimal risks like slight pain, minor bruising, or, rarely, feeling lightheaded. Serious complications are extremely uncommon.

faqs.question: What level of cholesterol test is normal?
faqs.answer: Normal total cholesterol is less than 200 mg/dL. Borderline high is 200-240 mg/dL, and high is 240 mg/dL or above. Your doctor will interpret results based on your overall health profile.

preparation: 3 ml of EDTA Blood in two EDTA tubes

name: BioFire Meningitis/Encephalitis Panel Test
preparation: Clinical history and clinician details must be mentioned on the test requisition form (TRF)

faqs.question: What does the BioFire Meningitis/Encephalitis Panel Test detect?
faqs.answer: It detects 14 major bacterial, viral, and fungal pathogens that cause meningitis and encephalitis using a CSF sample.

faqs.question: How is the sample collected?
faqs.answer: The test requires a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample collected via lumbar puncture by a doctor.

faqs.question: How soon are the results available?
faqs.answer: Results are available within approximately 10 hours after the sample is received at the lab.

faqs.question: Can this test identify both bacterial and viral causes?
faqs.answer: Yes, it detects both bacterial and viral agents simultaneously using multiplex PCR.

faqs.question: Is fasting required before the test?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required.

faqs.question: Can this test replace culture testing?
faqs.answer: No, it complements culture tests and should be interpreted with clinical and laboratory findings.

faqs.question: What does the T-ALL MRD Test measure?
faqs.answer: The T-ALL MRD Test analyze and quantify residual leukemic cells in the bone marrow or peripheral blood in patients with T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (T-ALL).

faqs.question: Why is the T-ALL MRD Test done?
faqs.answer: • To monitor treatment effectiveness in patients with T-ALL • To detect MRD after treatment • To assess the risk of disease recurrence

faqs.question: When is the T-ALL MRD Test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: The T-ALL MRD Test is recommended for patients with T-ALL.

faqs.question: What if the results of the T-ALL MRD Test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: If the T-ALL MRD Test results are abnormal, it may indicate residual cancer cells or a higher risk of disease recurrence.

faqs.question: What to expect during the T-ALL MRD Test?
faqs.answer: During the test, a sample of bone marrow is collected using a needle. The sample is sent to the laboratory for analysis using flow cytometry.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the T-ALL MRD Test?
faqs.answer: • Inform your doctor about any medications or supplements you are taking. Also, tell them if you have any specific requirements. • Provide your medical history and any relevant hemato-pathological reports to your doctor • Follow any additional instructions given by your doctor.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the T-ALL MRD Test?
faqs.answer: • Hemato-pathological reports: To provide a comprehensive understanding of the disease and monitor treatment response • Genetic testing: To identify specific genetic abnormalities associated with T-ALL

faqs.question: What is the T-ALL MRD Test also known as?
faqs.answer: Minimal residual disease test for T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (T-ALL)

faqs.question: What is T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia?
faqs.answer: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (T-ALL) is a type of blood cancer that affects immature T-cells. It is characterised by an overproduction of abnormal T-cells in the bone marrow.

faqs.question: What does the Indirect Coombs Test detect?
faqs.answer: It detects free antibodies in your bloodstream that may react with red blood cells, causing haemolysis or transfusion reactions.

faqs.question: Is the Indirect Coombs Test necessary before a blood
faqs.answer: Yes, it ensures that the donor blood is compatible with your own, preventing adverse

faqs.question: Why is the Indirect Coombs Test done during pregnancy?
faqs.answer: To check if an Rh-negative mother has developed antibodies against her baby’s Rh-positive blood cells.

faqs.question: Do I need to fast before the Indirect Coombs Test?
faqs.answer: No fasting is required for this test.

faqs.question: How is the Indirect Coombs Test performed?
faqs.answer: A blood sample is collected from your arm and analysed using Automated Column Agglutination Technology (CAT).

faqs.question: What does a positive Indirect Coombs Test result mean?
faqs.answer: It means antibodies are present that can react with red blood cells, indicating possible incompatibility or immune disorder.

faqs.question: Are there risks associated with this test?
faqs.answer: Minimal risks such as slight bruising or mild discomfort at the needle site.

faqs.question: What is a normal Indirect Coombs Test result?
faqs.answer: A normal result is negative, meaning no harmful antibodies were detected.

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the Chikungunya PCR Test?
faqs.answer: The test is most useful during the early phase of illness, especially within the first week after symptoms begin. Your doctor will advise the right timing based on your fever and symptom history.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the Chikungunya PCR Test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, overnight fasting is not required for the Chikungunya PCR Test. You can eat and drink normally unless your doctor has advised fasting for another test.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my Chikungunya PCR Test results?
faqs.answer: Mild dehydration usually does not directly affect chikungunya RNA detection. However, normal hydration is recommended before any blood test unless your doctor has restricted fluids.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the Chikungunya PCR Test?
faqs.answer: No special diet is needed. Inform your doctor about all medicines, fever medicines, painkillers, previous reports and treatment history before the test.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the Chikungunya PCR Test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional ties a tourniquet around your arm, cleans the puncture site, uses a sterile needle to collect blood for EDTA plasma testing, removes the needle and applies a bandage.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: The risks are minimal and similar to a routine blood test. You may feel slight pain, mild bruising, swelling or temporary discomfort at the needle site.

faqs.question: What does Chikungunya Virus RNA PCR Not Detected mean?
faqs.answer: It means chikungunya virus RNA was not detected in your blood sample. Your doctor will interpret this with your symptoms, timing of illness and other test results if needed.

name: Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing – Body Fluids

faqs.question: What does the Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing test measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence of fungal DNA, and thus, fungal infections, in body fluids by using a combination of molecular biology techniques to identify the DNA of various types of fungi.

faqs.question: Why is the Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing test done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose fungal infections in body fluids. • To guide treatment decisions and monitor the effectiveness of antifungal therapy. • To identify the specific type of fungi causing the infection, which helps determine the appropriate antifungal medications. • To differentiate between fungal infections and other conditions with similar symptoms.

faqs.question: When is the Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test may be recommended if you have • Symptoms suggestive of a fungal infection, such as fever, cough, skin rashes, or abnormal discharge. • A weakened immune system due to conditions such as HIV/AIDS or organ transplantation. • A known exposure to fungi or a high risk of fungal infections due to occupational or environmental factors.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate the presence of a fungal infection.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing test?
faqs.answer: Your healthcare provider will collect a sample of your body fluid, such as blood, cerebrospinal fluid, or pleural fluid. The sample will be sent to the laboratory for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing test?
faqs.answer: There are no specific preparations required for this test. However, it is essential to provide accurate clinical information and mention the type of body fluid being tested on the Test Request Form (TRF) for proper diagnosis. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing test?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside Panfungal-DNA detection include: • Fungal culture: This test helps grow and identify fungi present in a sample. • Antifungal susceptibility testing: It determines which antifungal medications are most effective against the identified fungi. • Histopathology: Microscopic examination of tissue samples to detect fungal elements and evaluate the extent of infection.

faqs.question: What is the Panfungal-DNA Detection by PCR & Sanger Sequencing test also known as?
faqs.answer: This test is also known as Panfungal Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) and Sanger Sequencing.

faqs.question: What is a fungal infection?
faqs.answer: A fungal infection is caused by various types of fungi, which are microscopic organisms commonly found in the environment. Fungal infections can affect different parts of the body, including the skin, nails, lungs, and bloodstream, causing a range of symptoms and complications.

faqs.question: What does the Prothrombin G20210A (Factor II) Mutation test measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence of the Prothrombin G20210A mutation in the FII gene.

faqs.question: Why is the Prothrombin G20210A (Factor II) Mutation test done?
faqs.answer: This test helps identify individuals at an increased risk of developing blood clots. It is mainly done to • Assess the risk of developing blood clots. • Assess the risk of venous thrombosis. • Inform appropriate preventive measures and treatment plans.

faqs.question: When is the Prothrombin G20210A (Factor II) Mutation test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Doctors may recommend this test for • Individuals with a personal or family history of venous thrombosis, • Individuals who are taking oral contraceptives and have experienced a venous thrombotic event. • Pregnant women.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Prothrombin G20210A (Factor II) Mutation test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results, i.e., reports indicating that the mutation is present, mean that there is an increased risk of developing blood clots. Abnormal results do not necessarily mean you have a clot or a serious condition, but it's important to discuss them with your doctor for further evaluation and appropriate management.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Prothrombin G20210A (Factor II) Mutation test?
faqs.answer: For this test: • A sample of 3-5 ml of your EDTA whole blood will be required. • The collection procedure is quick and simple, involving a blood draw.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Prothrombin G20210A (Factor II) Mutation test?
faqs.answer: To prepare for this test: • No fasting or special diet is needed. • Make sure to inform your doctor about any medications you are taking, as certain drugs can interfere with the test results. • Follow any additional instructions given by your doctor regarding medications or other preparations. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Prothrombin G20210A (Factor II) Mutation test?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside the Prothrombin G20210A (Factor II) Mutation test include: • Complete Blood Count (CBC): This test evaluates different components of your blood, including red and white blood cells, to assess overall blood health. • Coagulation Panel: This panel includes various tests to evaluate clotting factors and assess the overall functioning of the coagulation system.

faqs.question: What is the Prothrombin G20210A (Factor II) Mutation test also known as?
faqs.answer: FII G20210A Mutation test, Prothrombin Gene Mutation test

faqs.question: What is venous thrombosis?
faqs.answer: Venous thrombosis refers to the formation of blood clots in the veins, usually in the legs or pelvis. It can cause pain, swelling, and potentially serious complications if the clot dislodges and travels to other parts of the body.

name: AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Clofazimine Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex

faqs.question: What does AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Clofazimine Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex measure?
faqs.answer: This test determines the susceptibility of the MTb complex to the drug Clofazimine.

faqs.question: Why is AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Clofazimine Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex done?
faqs.answer: • This test is primarily done to understand the drug susceptibility of the MTb complex specifically to clofazimine by assessing the growth patterns of MTb complex bacteria in response to this drug. • Additionally, it allows healthcare professionals to monitor drug resistance patterns and adjust treatment plans accordingly.

faqs.question: When is AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Clofazimine Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended in the following circumstances: • Patients with confirmed or suspected tuberculosis infections to determine the most appropriate drug regimen • Individuals who have shown resistance or intolerance to other tuberculosis medications • Those requiring a change in their current medication due to treatment failure or recurrence of TB

faqs.question: What if the results of the AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Clofazimine Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate resistance to Clofazimine, which could affect the choice of medication.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Clofazimine Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex?
faqs.answer: Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Clofazimine Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside this test include: • Drug susceptibility testing for other drugs used in tuberculosis treatment • Chest X-ray or CT scan to evaluate the extent of lung involvement • Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear and culture tests to confirm the presence of mycobacteria and identify the specific strain

faqs.question: What is the AFB (TB) – Antibiogram for MTb Complex – Clofazimine Drug by MGIT – Pure Growth of MTB Complex also known as?
faqs.answer: Clofazimine Antibiogram for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTb) complex using MGIT method

faqs.question: What is tuberculosis (TB)?
faqs.answer: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease caused by the Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacteria. It primarily affects the lungs, but can also impact other organs. TB spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Symptoms include persistent cough, weight loss, fever, and fatigue. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent complications and transmission.

faqs.question: What does the CD34 Test – Haematology measure?
faqs.answer: The CD34 Test detect the presence of CD34 antigen on hematopoietic stem cells and precursor cells.

faqs.question: Why is the CD34 Test – Haematology done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose and monitor precursor leukaemia • To determine the extent, severity, and progression of the disease and assess treatment response • To guide treatment decisions, such as the need for stem cell transplantation • To evaluate the prognosis (outlook) for patients with precursor leukaemia

faqs.question: When is the CD34 Test – Haematology recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: The CD34 Test – Haematology is recommended in the following situations: • When a patient shows symptoms suggestive of precursor leukaemia, such as unexplained fatigue, frequent infections, or easy bleeding/bruising • For those already diagnosed with precursor leukaemia to assess the stage and progression of the disease • To monitor treatment response and detect relapse in patients with precursor leukaemia • Before planning a stem cell transplantation for precursor leukaemia patients.

faqs.question: What if the results of the CD34 Test – Haematology are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal result may indicate precursor leukaemia.

faqs.question: What to expect during the CD34 Test – Haematology?
faqs.answer: During the CD34 Test – Haematology: • A small sample (3 ml) of your blood is collected using a needle. • The sample is sent to the laboratory for analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the CD34 Test – Haematology?
faqs.answer: Before the CD34 Test – Haematology: • No specific preparations are required. • Inform your doctor about any medications you are taking or medical conditions you have that may affect the test results. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the CD34 Test – Haematology?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside the CD34 Test – Haematology include: • Complete blood count (CBC): To evaluate other blood cell counts and identify any abnormalities • Bone marrow biopsy: To obtain a sample of bone marrow for further analysis, if leukaemia is suspected. • Genetic testing: To assess specific genetic abnormalities associated with precursor leukaemia or guide treatment decisions.

faqs.question: What is the CD34 Test – Haematology also known as?
faqs.answer: CD34 immunophenotyping test, flow cytometry immunophenotyping for precursor leukaemia

faqs.question: What is precursor leukaemia?
faqs.answer: Precursor leukaemia, also known as acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) or acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), is a type of blood cancer that affects immature blood cells, including stem cells. It is characterised by uncontrolled growth and accumulation of these abnormal cells in the bone marrow and bloodstream.

name: Biotinidase Activity Neonatal Dried Blood Spot
Thyroglobulin Test
preparation: Avoid high-dose biotin supplements (more than 5 mg/day) for at least 8 hours before blood collection

faqs.question: What does the Thyroglobulin test measure?
faqs.answer: It measures the level of thyroglobulin protein in your blood to monitor thyroid cancer treatment and detect recurrence.

faqs.question: Is fasting required for the Thyroglobulin test?
faqs.answer: Fasting not required; you can eat and drink normally before the test.

faqs.question: When is the Thyroglobulin test recommended?
faqs.answer: It is done after thyroid surgery or radioactive iodine therapy to monitor treatment success and recurrence.

faqs.question: Can biotin affect my Thyroglobulin test results?
faqs.answer: Yes, high-dose biotin supplements can interfere. Avoid them at least 8 hours before testing.

faqs.question: What do high Thyroglobulin levels mean?
faqs.answer: High levels may indicate remaining thyroid tissue, cancer recurrence, or metastasis.

faqs.question: What do low Thyroglobulin levels indicate?
faqs.answer: Low or undetectable levels suggest effective thyroid cancer treatment and no residual tissue.

faqs.question: Can I take my regular medicines before the test?
faqs.answer: Yes, but inform your doctor about all medications or supplements you’re taking.

faqs.question: How often should I do the Thyroglobulin test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor will decide the frequency, often every 6–12 months after thyroid cancer treatment.<

faqs.question: Why take HLA typing DQ locus Class II Test?
faqs.answer: This test is done to rule diseases strongly linked to DQ locus. For e.g., coeliac disease, narcolepsy

faqs.question: Is this test for you?
faqs.answer: Performed for patients suspected of having diseases strongly associated with the HLA-DQ locus for e.g. coeliac disease

faqs.question: More Info on HLA typing DQ locus Class II Test
faqs.answer: Celiac disease (CD) is a multifactorial immune-mediated disease.Specific HLA-DQ genes have been recognized as necessary factors for the occurrence of Celiac Disease (CD). This test provides genotyping for detection of HLA-DQ2 (DQA1*05:01 or 05:05 and DQB1*02:01 or 02:02) and HLA-DQ8 (DQB1*03:02). The HLA-DQB1*02:01 allele is present in more than 90% CD children. In the perspective of a widened pediatric population screening for CD, a double-step process might be suggested: HLA-DQB1*02:01 might be investigated first and, only if this result is positive, children might be candidate for a prospective serologic screening, as a second step

name: Allergen, Individual-Animal Guinea Pig Epithelium Serum

faqs.question: What does the Allergy Adult Panel 3 test detect?
faqs.answer: It identifies specific allergens such as dust, food, pollen, and animal dander that may trigger allergic reactions in adults.

faqs.question: Is fasting required before taking the Allergy Adult Panel 3 test?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required. You can eat and drink as usual before your appointment.

faqs.question: Can medications affect my Allergy Adult Panel 3 test results?
faqs.answer: Yes, antihistamines or steroids can reduce your allergic response. Inform your doctor about all medicines you take before testing.

faqs.question: How is the sample collected for the Allergy Adult Panel 3 test?
faqs.answer: A small blood sample is drawn from your arm, processed in the lab, and analysed using the immunoblot method.

faqs.question: What are the risks associated with the test?
faqs.answer: Risks are minimal, limited to slight pain or bruising at the puncture site, which usually resolves quickly.

faqs.question: What does a high IgE level mean in the Allergy Adult Panel 3 test?
faqs.answer: High IgE levels indicate your immune system is sensitised to one or more allergens and reacting abnormally to their presence.

faqs.question: Can the Allergy Adult Panel 3 test identify food allergies?
faqs.answer: Yes, it detects IgE-mediated reactions to foods like milk, nuts, seafood, and grains.

faqs.question: How reliable is the Allergy Adult Panel 3 test?
faqs.answer: It uses advanced MAST immunoblot technology, offering high accuracy and reproducibility in identifying allergic sensitisation.

name: Chromogranin A (CGA) Test - Serum
preparation:

Show More

faqs.question: What does a high Chromogranin A level mean?
faqs.answer: High levels may indicate a neuroendocrine tumour or can occur due to medications like PPIs or non-cancerous diseases.

faqs.question: Is fasting required for the Chromogranin A Test?
faqs.answer: Fasting is not mandatory, but avoid heavy meals or caffeine before the test.

faqs.question: Can medication affect my Chromogranin A Test results?
faqs.answer: Yes. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) and acid-reducing medicines can cause false elevations. Discuss alternatives with your doctor before the test.

faqs.question: Can this test detect all types of neuroendocrine tumours?
faqs.answer: It can detect most NETs but is not specific for tumour location; imaging tests may be needed for confirmation.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get the test results?
faqs.answer: Reports are generally available on the same day by 9:00 PM once the sample reaches the lab.

faqs.question: What are neuroendocrine tumours?
faqs.answer: They are rare tumours that develop from hormone-producing nerve cells found in the pancreas, GI tract, and adrenal glands.

faqs.question: Can I continue taking my medicines before the test?
faqs.answer: Avoid PPIs for at least 2 weeks before the test if possible. Always consult your doctor before stopping any medication.

name: Fungal Culture And Identification By MALDITOF (Vitek MS) - Hair

faqs.question: What does the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - Hair measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence of fungal infections in hair samples.

faqs.question: Why is the Fungal Culture and Identification test - Hair done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose fungal infections in the hair • To provide appropriate antifungal treatment • To monitor the effectiveness of antifungal treatment • To identify specific fungal species causing the infection

faqs.question: When is the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - Hair recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended for individuals who • exhibit symptoms such as persistent scalp itching, scaling, or hair loss, • have a suspected fungal infection based on their medical history or physical examination, or • require treatment with antifungal medication for a diagnosed fungal infection.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - Hair are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate the presence of a fungal infection in the hair.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Fungal Culture and Identification test - Hair?
faqs.answer: During this test, a healthcare professional will collect a sample of your hair in a sterile, leak-proof container. They will send your hair sample to the laboratory for analysis using automated MALDITOF technology.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Fungal Culture and Identification Test - Hair?
faqs.answer: • Follow any specific instructions provided by your doctor. • Inform your doctor if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Fungal Culture and Identification Test- Hair?
faqs.answer: • KOH (Potassium Hydroxide) preparation: This test helps visualise fungal elements under a microscope. • Histopathology: This test examines hair samples under a microscope to identify fungal infections.

faqs.question: What is the Fungal Culture and Identification Test- Hair also known as?
faqs.answer: Hair Fungal Culture and Identification or Hair Mycology

faqs.question: What is the significance of diagnosing fungal infections in hair?
faqs.answer: Fungal infections in hair can lead to various conditions such as scalp ringworm (tinea capitis) or fungal folliculitis. Accurate diagnosis through tests helps ensure appropriate treatment and prevents further complications.

name: Chlamydia Trachomatis DNA Detection by Real Time PCR

faqs.question: What does a positive VZV IgG test mean?
faqs.answer: A positive result indicates that you have antibodies against Varicella Zoster Virus, suggesting past infection or successful vaccination.

faqs.question: Can this test detect a current chickenpox infection?
faqs.answer: The IgG test mainly shows past exposure or immunity. For active infection, your doctor may recommend a VZV IgM or PCR test.

faqs.question: Is fasting needed before the VZV test?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required. You can eat and drink as usual.

faqs.question: Can the test be done during pregnancy?
faqs.answer: Yes, the VZV test is often recommended during pregnancy to ensure you are immune to chickenpox and to prevent infection risks.

faqs.question: What should I tell my doctor before the test?
faqs.answer: Inform your doctor about any ongoing medications, immune-related conditions, or if you recently received a vaccine.

name: AFB (TB) - Antibiogram For MTb Complex - Moxifloxacin Drug By MGIT - Pure Growth Of MTB Complex

faqs.question: What does AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Moxifloxacin measure?
faqs.answer: This test measures the drug susceptibility of tuberculosis (TB) to the antibiotic moxifloxacin.

faqs.question: Why is AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Moxifloxacin done?
faqs.answer: • To identify drug-resistant strains of TB bacteria • To guide appropriate treatment decisions • To monitor the effectiveness of moxifloxacin in treating TB

faqs.question: When is AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Moxifloxacin recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended for • suspected or confirmed cases of tuberculosis, • identification of drug-resistant strains, • monitoring treatment progress and response to moxifloxacin, or • patients with a history of non-compliance to TB medications.

faqs.question: What if the results of the AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Moxifloxacin are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate drug resistance, requiring alternate antibiotics for effective treatment.

faqs.question: What to expect during the AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Moxifloxacin?

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Moxifloxacin?

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Moxifloxacin?
faqs.answer: • AFB smear microscopy: This test helps in the initial detection of TB bacteria in sputum or other clinical specimens. • Drug susceptibility testing: This determines the susceptibility of TB bacteria to various antibiotics.

faqs.question: What is AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Moxifloxacin also known as?
faqs.answer: TB drug susceptibility testing for moxifloxacin

faqs.question: What is Tuberculosis (TB)?
