AFB (TB) - Antibiogram For MTb Complex - Rifampicin Drug By MGIT - Pure Growth Of MTB Complex

faqs.question: What does AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Rifampicin measure?
faqs.answer: AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Rifampicin measures the drug susceptibility of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (the bacteria that causes TB) to the antibiotic Rifampicin.

faqs.question: Why is AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Rifampicin done?
faqs.answer: • To determine if Mycobacterium tuberculosis is resistant to Rifampicin, aiding in effective treatment selection • To assess the drug susceptibility pattern of TB to ensure appropriate and timely therapy • To monitor the emergence of drug resistance during TB treatment

faqs.question: When is AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Rifampicin recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended • when a patient is diagnosed with tuberculosis and needs drug susceptibility testing, • if a patient has previously been treated for tuberculosis but shows signs of recurrent or persistent infection, or • for patients at high risk of drug-resistant TB, such as those with a history of non-compliance with treatment or exposure to someone with drug-resistant TB.

faqs.question: What if the results of the AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Rifampicin are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results may indicate resistance to Rifampicin, suggesting the need for alternative drug choices.

faqs.question: What to expect during the AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Rifampicin?
faqs.answer: During this test, a healthcare professional will take a sample of your Tuberculosis bacteria. They will test this sample using the MGIT method to determine drug susceptibility.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Rifampicin?
faqs.answer: • Follow any instructions provided by your healthcare provider regarding dietary restrictions or medication adjustments. • Inform your doctor if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Rifampicin?
faqs.answer: • AFB smear and culture: These tests are used to initially detect and identify Mycobacterium tuberculosis. • Genotypic testing: :ine probe assays or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) can identify specific genetic mutations associated with drug resistance.

faqs.question: What is AFB (TB) Antibiogram - Rifampicin also known as?
faqs.answer: TB drug susceptibility testing for Rifampicin or TB antibiotic sensitivity testing for Rifampicin

faqs.question: What is tuberculosis (TB)?
faqs.answer: Tuberculosis is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It primarily affects the lungs but can also affect other parts of the body.

name: HIV-1 RNA Viral load by Taqman RT PCR
Maternal Screen (Triple Test) Second Trimester Test
preparation: Completely filled maternal TRF with barcode and latest USG report required. History is mandatory

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the Maternal Screen (Triple Test) Second Trimester Test?
faqs.answer: The test is recommended between 14 and 22.6 weeks of pregnancy, ideally between 15 and 17 weeks for better reliability.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the Maternal Screen (Triple Test) Second Trimester Test, and for how long?
faqs.answer: Fasting is not required. You can eat and drink normally before the test.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my Maternal Screen (Triple Test) Second Trimester Test results?
faqs.answer: Severe dehydration is unlikely to significantly affect results, but maintaining normal hydration is always advisable before any blood test.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the Maternal Screen (Triple Test) Second Trimester Test?
faqs.answer: No special diet is needed. Inform your doctor about any medical conditions and ensure accurate gestational age details are provided.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the Maternal Screen (Triple Test) Second Trimester Test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional collects about 3 ml of blood from a vein in your arm using standard sterile technique.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: Risks are minimal and similar to any routine blood test. You may experience mild pain or slight bruising at the needle site.

faqs.question: What level of Maternal Screen (Triple Test) Second Trimester Test is normal?
faqs.answer: Results are reported as risk ratios and MoM values. A screen negative result indicates low risk, while a screen positive result suggests higher risk and may require further testing.

name: JC-BK Virus DNA Detection by Real-time PCR - Urine

faqs.question: What does JC-BK Virus DNA Detection by Real-time PCR - Urine measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence of JC polyoma and BK virus in your urine using the Real-Time PCR method.

faqs.question: Why is JC-BK Virus DNA Detection by Real-time PCR - Urine done?
faqs.answer: • To detect the presence of JC polyoma and BK viruses • To help patients with weakened immune systems due to conditions such as HIV • To oversee the immunity of people who have had an organ transplant or are undergoing chemotherapy

faqs.question: When is JC-BK Virus DNA Detection test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend this test if you have • a weakened immune system due to conditions such as HIV, • had an organ transplant or are undergoing chemotherapy, or • symptoms such as fever, urinary tract infections, or other symptoms suggestive of viral infections.

faqs.question: What if the results of the JC-BK Virus DNA Detection urine test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: If you test positive for JC polyoma or BK virus, it may indicate an active or past infection.

faqs.question: What to expect during the JC-BK Virus DNA Detection test?
faqs.answer: You will be asked to collect a 15ml spot urine sample in a sterile leak-proof container. The sample will be sent to the laboratory for testing.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the JC-BK Virus DNA Detection test?
faqs.answer: • Inform your doctor about any medications you are taking. • Follow any other instructions provided by your doctor and let them know if you have any specific requirements. • Provide details of your clinical history and clinician number.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the JC-BK Virus DNA Detection test?
faqs.answer: Blood tests to check kidney function and overall health.

faqs.question: What is the JC-BK Virus DNA Detection by Real-time PCR - Urine also known as?
faqs.answer: Polyomavirus JC/BK DNA Quantitative PCR, JC and BK Virus, or JC/BK Quantitative Real-Time PCR

faqs.question: What are JC polyoma and BK viruses?
faqs.answer: JC polyoma and BK virus are common viruses that usually do not cause symptoms in healthy people. However, they can cause serious infections in people suffering from conditions such as HIV, organ transplant, or chemotherapy.

name: Lead (Blood
preparation: Avoid environmental contamination during sample collection

faqs.question: What does the Lead Blood Test check for?
faqs.answer: It measures the amount of lead in your blood to detect exposure or poisoning.

faqs.question: Do I need to fast before the test?
faqs.answer: Fasting not required. You can eat and drink normally.

faqs.question: What does a high lead level mean?
faqs.answer: High levels indicate lead exposure that may require treatment or environmental investigation.

faqs.question: Who should get tested for lead?
faqs.answer: Children, industrial workers, and anyone exposed to contaminated paint, soil, or water.

faqs.question: How is the sample collected?
faqs.answer: A blood sample is drawn into a special K?EDTA tube using sterile, metal-free equipment.

faqs.question: What should I do if my lead levels are high?
faqs.answer: Consult your doctor for treatment and identify possible lead sources in your environment.

faqs.question: What do high Cardiolipin IgM levels indicate?
faqs.answer: High Cardiolipin IgM levels suggest the presence of autoimmune activity, which may increase the risk of blood clots and pregnancy loss, often linked to Antiphospholipid Syndrome (APS) or lupus.

faqs.question: Can I eat before a Cardiolipin Antibody Test?
faqs.answer: Yes, fasting is not required. You may eat and drink as usual before the test.

faqs.question: What other tests are done along with the Cardiolipin Antibody Test?
faqs.answer: Doctors may recommend Beta-2-Glycoprotein IgG Antibody, Lupus Anticoagulant Test, or other autoimmune screening tests for complete evaluation.

faqs.question: How is the blood sample collected for this test?
faqs.answer: A trained professional ties a tourniquet on your arm, cleans the site, and draws about 3 ml of blood into a gel vacutainer for testing.

faqs.question: Are there any risks associated with this test?
faqs.answer: The risks are minimal. You may feel slight pain or bruising at the puncture site, which usually resolves quickly.

faqs.question: What is considered a normal result for this test?
faqs.answer: A result below 15 MPL U/mL is considered normal, indicating no significant autoimmune antibody activity.

faqs.question: Can temporary illness affect my Cardiolipin Antibody levels?
faqs.answer: Yes, temporary infections or inflammatory conditions can cause short-term rises in antibody levels. Persistent positivity confirmed after 12 weeks is considered clinically significant.

name: BCR ABL FISH Test - Bcr-Abl (PHILADELPHIA) t(9 22) by FISH Test

faqs.question: Why take Bcr-Abl (PHILADELPHIA) t(9 22) by FISH Test?
faqs.answer: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) using BCR/ABL 1 probe is useful in the identification of the Philadelphia chromosome in patients with CML, ALL, or AML.

faqs.question: Is this test for you?
faqs.answer: Doctors may prescribe this test in certain types of blood cancers like CML, ALL, AML for diagnosis and managenemt.

faqs.question: More Info on Bcr-Abl (PHILADELPHIA) t(9 22) by FISH Test
faqs.answer: This test is performed to detect the chromosomal abnormalities of the BCR and ABL1 genes involved in translocation t(9;22) associated with chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML), acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) using FISH. FISH is useful in monitoring remission in patient, diagnosing leukemia; as a target of therapuetic drugs, to measure objective response to chemotherapyand also helps in decision making to increase drug dose or to change to a second-line treatment.

faqs.question: What is the Stool Culture & Sensitivity Test used for?
faqs.answer: It detects harmful bacteria in stool samples and determines which antibiotics are effective for treatment.

faqs.question: Do I need to fast before this test?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required.

faqs.question: How long does the test take?
faqs.answer: Reports are available after 4 days.

faqs.question: What are common bacteria detected in this test?
faqs.answer: Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli, Vibrio species, and Campylobacter.

faqs.question: Can antibiotics affect the result?
faqs.answer: Yes, taking antibiotics before the test may suppress bacterial growth and alter results.

faqs.question: How is the sample collected?
faqs.answer: Collect about 5 grams of stool in a sterile container provided by the lab. Avoid contamination with urine or water.

faqs.question: How do I interpret the report?
faqs.answer: A “No Growth” result indicates no infection, while growth of specific bacteria confirms an infection and includes antibiotic sensitivity details.

name: Vitamin B6 Test
preparation: Avoid taking vitamin B6 supplements for at least 24 hours before the test

faqs.question: What does the Vitamin B6 Test check for?
faqs.answer: It measures the level of pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), the active form of vitamin B6, to assess deficiency or excess affecting nerves and metabolism.

faqs.question: Should I stop taking supplements before the test?
faqs.answer: Yes, avoid taking vitamin B6 supplements for at least 24 hours before the test to ensure accuracy.

faqs.question: Is fasting required for the Vitamin B6 Test?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required. You can eat and drink normally before your test.

faqs.question: How is the Vitamin B6 Test performed?
faqs.answer: A small blood sample is drawn from your vein into a light-protected EDTA tube and tested using HPLC technology.

faqs.question: What are the symptoms of low vitamin B6?
faqs.answer: Fatigue, tingling in hands or feet, cracked lips, mood changes, and poor immunity may indicate deficiency.

faqs.question: Can medications affect my Vitamin B6 levels?
faqs.answer: Yes, drugs such as isoniazid, cyclosporine, and penicillamine can lower your vitamin B6 levels.

faqs.question: What is the normal range for Vitamin B6 levels?
faqs.answer: Normal values typically range between 8.7 – 27.2 ng/mL.

faqs.question: What does a high Vitamin B6 level mean?
faqs.answer: High levels usually indicate excessive supplement intake and can lead to nerve-related toxicity.

Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Sputum

faqs.question: What does the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Sputum test measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence of fungi in a sputum sample obtained from the respiratory system and identifies the specific type of fungus using MALDITOF technology.

faqs.question: Why is the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Sputum test done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose fungal infections in the respiratory system. • To determine the specific type of fungus causing the infection. • To guide clinicians in prescribing appropriate antifungal treatment. • To monitor the effectiveness of antifungal treatment. • To assess the risk of developing fungal infections for individuals with certain risk factors.

faqs.question: When is the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Sputum test recommended, and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test may be recommended if you • Have symptoms such as persistent cough, chest pain, or shortness of breath that could indicate a fungal infection. • Have a compromised immune system, such as due to HIV/AIDS or organ transplantation. • Have been exposed to environments where fungal infections are common, such as construction sites or agricultural settings.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Sputum test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results indicate the presence of fungal infection in the respiratory system.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Sputum test?
faqs.answer: You will be asked to provide a sputum sample in a sterile container. The sample will then be sent to the laboratory for processing.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Sputum test?
faqs.answer: Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Sputum test?
faqs.answer: • Blood tests to assess immune function and identify specific antibodies against fungal infections. • Imaging tests such as chest X-rays or CT scans to evaluate the extent of lung involvement. • Biopsy of lung tissue if needed for further evaluation.

faqs.question: What is the Fungal Culture and Identification by MALDITOF (Vitek MS) – Sputum test also known as?
faqs.answer: Fungal Culture and Identification using MALDITOF (Vitek MS) technology Sputum

faqs.question: What is a fungal infection?
faqs.answer: Fungal infections are caused by various types of fungi and can affect different parts of the body, including the respiratory system. Common fungal infections include aspergillosis, candidiasis, and histoplasmosis. Early detection and appropriate treatment are essential for managing these infections effectively.

faqs.question: What does RSV-IgM Antibody by EIA - Serum measure?
faqs.answer: This test measures the levels of specific IgM antibodies that are produced by your immune system in response to RSV infection.

faqs.question: Why is RSV-IgM Antibody by EIA - Serum done?
faqs.answer: • To detect specific IgM antibodies against the Respiratory syncytial virus • To determine the presence of an active RSV infection in high-risk individuals, such as newborns and immunocompromised patients

faqs.question: When is the RSV-IgM Antibody test recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend this test if you have • symptoms of respiratory illness like cold, cough, fever, or breathing difficulties, • comorbidities like asthma, lung diseases, or cardiac conditions that can exacerbate RSV infection, or • a weakened immune system or congenital heart defects.

faqs.question: What if the results of the RSV-IgM Antibody test are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal results indicating high levels of IgM antibodies may suggest a recent RSV infection.

faqs.question: What to expect during the RSV-IgM Antibody Serum test?
faqs.answer: A healthcare professional will draw a sample of your blood from a vein in your arm. The blood sample will then be sent to a laboratory for testing.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the RSV-IgM Antibody Serum test?
faqs.answer: Inform your doctor if you're taking any medication or have any medical conditions that can interfere with the test results. Also, tell them if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the RSV-IgM Antibody test?
faqs.answer: RSV antigen detection: This test helps to identify the virus directly in body fluids like nasal discharge or blood.

faqs.question: What is the RSV-IgM Antibody by EIA - Serum also known as?
faqs.answer: Respiratory Syncytial Virus IgM antibody, RSV IgM ELISA, or RSV Ab IgM EIA

faqs.question: What is Respiratory Syncytial Virus?
faqs.answer: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) is a common cause of respiratory illness, primarily in young children. It's highly contagious and can cause a wide range of symptoms from mild cold-like symptoms to severe bronchiolitis and pneumonia in high-risk individuals.

name: Infectious Mononucleosis Profile by IFA - Serum

faqs.question: What does Infectious Mononucleosis Profile measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects the presence of Infectious Mononucleosis (IM) heterophile antibodies in your blood, which are produced in response to the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).

faqs.question: Why is Infectious Mononucleosis Profile done?
faqs.answer: • To detect IM heterophile antibodies in serum • To confirm a suspected diagnosis of infectious mononucleosis • To assess the stage of the infection • To monitor the effectiveness of treatment • To rule out other conditions that have similar symptoms

faqs.question: When is Infectious Mononucleosis Profile recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor might recommend this test if you have • symptoms suggestive of infectious mononucleosis such as fever, sore throat, swollen lymph nodes, and fatigue, • suspected exposure to EBV, • complications suggestive of infectious mononucleosis such as enlargement of the spleen or liver, or • immunosuppression or a weakened immune system.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Infectious Mononucleosis Profile are abnormal?
faqs.answer: An elevated level of heterophile antibodies indicates the presence of EBV infection leading to infectious mononucleosis.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Infectious Mononucleosis Profile - Serum?
faqs.answer: This test requires a blood sample to be drawn from your arm. The sample will be then sent to a laboratory for testing.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Infectious Mononucleosis Profile?
faqs.answer: • Inform your healthcare provider of any medications that you are taking. • Avoid certain medications before the test because they can interfere with the results. • Inform your doctor if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with Infectious Mononucleosis Profile?
faqs.answer: • Complete blood count (CBC) to measure white blood cells count • Liver function tests (LFTs) to assess liver function • EBV DNA polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test to detect EBV DNA.

faqs.question: What is Infectious Mononucleosis Profile also known as?
faqs.answer: Heterophile Antibody Test or Rapid Mono Test

faqs.question: What is infectious mononucleosis?
faqs.answer: Infectious mononucleosis is a viral infection caused by EBV. It spreads through saliva and close contact with an infected person. Symptoms include fever, sore throat, fatigue, swollen lymph nodes, and enlarged spleen or liver.

faqs.question: What does a positive LAC test mean?
faqs.answer: A positive result indicates the presence of lupus anticoagulant antibodies, suggesting increased risk of blood clots or pregnancy loss.

faqs.question: Do I need to fast before a LAC test?
faqs.answer: No fasting is required for this test.

faqs.question: Can medications affect my LAC test results?
faqs.answer: Yes. Anticoagulants like heparin or warfarin can interfere with results. Inform your doctor about all medications.

faqs.question: How is the LAC test performed?
faqs.answer: A blood sample is collected and tested using clotting assays such as aPTT and DRVV to detect lupus anticoagulant.

faqs.question: Can a LAC test confirm lupus?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. While lupus anticoagulant can occur in lupus, it may also appear in APS or other autoimmune conditions.

faqs.question: What is the normal range for DRVV screen ratio?
faqs.answer: The normal DRVV screen ratio ranges from 0.85 to 1.20. A value above 1.2 suggests lupus anticoagulant presence.

faqs.question: How often should the test be repeated?
faqs.answer: If positive, it should be repeated after 12 weeks to confirm persistent lupus anticoagulant.

faqs.question: Are there any risks with the test?
faqs.answer: Risks are minimal and include slight bruising or discomfort at the puncture site.

faqs.question: What is the best time to take the Drug Panel - Comprehensive (35Drugs), Serum?
faqs.answer: You can take this test when your doctor recommends it after a suspected drug reaction. Testing is most useful when your reaction history, timing and suspected medicine details are clearly shared with your doctor.

faqs.question: Is overnight fasting mandatory for the Drug Panel - Comprehensive (35Drugs), Serum, and for how long?
faqs.answer: No, overnight fasting is not required. You can eat and drink normally before the test unless your doctor has advised fasting for another test.

faqs.question: Can dehydration affect my Drug Panel - Comprehensive (35Drugs), Serum results?
faqs.answer: Mild dehydration usually does not directly affect drug specific IgE results. However, normal hydration can make blood collection easier and more comfortable.

faqs.question: How should I prepare my diet and medications before the Drug Panel - Comprehensive (35Drugs), Serum?
faqs.answer: No special diet is needed. Inform your doctor about all medicines, supplements, injections and previous drug reactions. Do not stop or restart any medicine unless your doctor advises you.

faqs.question: How is the blood draw procedure performed for the Drug Panel - Comprehensive (35Drugs), Serum?
faqs.answer: A phlebotomist cleans the skin, inserts a sterile needle into a vein in your arm and collects about 3 ml of blood in a gel vacutainer. The sample is then sent to the lab for EIA testing.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: The risks are minimal and similar to any routine blood test. You may feel slight pain, mild bruising, or dizziness during or after sample collection. Serious complications are rare.

faqs.question: What level of Drug Panel - Comprehensive (35Drugs), Serum is normal?
faqs.answer: A result below 0.36 IU/mL is reported as negative and clinically insignificant for the tested drug allergen. A result of 0.36 IU/mL or above is positive and should be interpreted by your doctor with your reaction history.

name: CLL Prognostication/Risk Stratification Gene Panel - EDTA Whole Blood

faqs.question: What does CLL Prognostication Gene Panel measure?
faqs.answer: CLL Prognostication Gene Panel analyzes specific genes associated with CLL that helps in predicting disease progression, treatment response, and overall patient outcomes.

faqs.question: Why is CLL Prognostication Gene Panel done?
faqs.answer: • To assess the risk stratification and prognosis of CLL • To guide treatment decisions by identifying high-risk patients who may require more aggressive therapies • To determine eligibility for clinical trials or targeted therapies based on specific gene mutations

faqs.question: When is CLL Prognostication Gene Panel recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: CLL Prognostication Gene Panel is recommended for individuals with • newly diagnosed CLL to evaluate risk stratification and determine appropriate treatment plans, • recurring or persistent CLL to assess disease progression and guide further therapeutic interventions, or • high-risk features such as unexplained cytopenias or rapid lymphocyte doubling time.

faqs.question: What if the results of the CLL Prognostication Gene Panel are abnormal?
faqs.answer: If the results of the CLL Prognostication Gene Panel show abnormalities, it may indicate a higher-risk profile for CLL. Abnormalities in specific genes can suggest a more aggressive disease course and may influence treatment decisions.

faqs.question: What to expect during the CLL Prognostication Gene Panel?
faqs.answer: During the test, a small sample of whole blood or bone marrow aspirate will be collected. The sample will be sent to a laboratory for Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) analysis.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the CLL Prognostication Gene Panel?
faqs.answer: • Fill out the genetic history form. • Follow any dietary or medication restrictions provided by your doctor. • Provide any relevant medical reports or imaging studies related to CLL or other related conditions. • Inform your doctor if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with CLL Prognostication Gene Panel?
faqs.answer: • Complete Blood Count (CBC): To assess blood cell counts and evaluate the extent of bone marrow involvement • Flow Cytometry: To determine the immunophenotypic profile of CLL cells • Cytogenetic Analysis: To identify chromosomal abnormalities associated with CLL

faqs.question: What is the CLL Prognostication Gene Panel also known as?
faqs.answer: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia Genetic Testing

faqs.question: What is chronic lymphocytic leukaemia?
faqs.answer: Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia is a cancer affecting white blood cells. It is characterised by uncontrolled growth and accumulation of abnormal lymphocytes in the blood, bone marrow, and lymph nodes.

name: Cell Free DNA For EGFR (Del19, L858R, T790M), Blood
AFB-DNA (TB-PCR) Detection by Real Time PCR – CSF

faqs.question: What does AFB-DNA (TB-PCR) Detection by Real Time PCR – CSF measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects DNA of Mycobacterium tuberculosis or non-tuberculous bacteria in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). If the result is MTB positive, the reflex test of Rifampicin resistance by Ultra CBNAAT is performed to determine if the MTB strain is resistant to Rifampicin, a critical drug used in TB treatment.

faqs.question: Why is AFB-DNA (TB-PCR) Detection by Real Time PCR – CSF done?
faqs.answer: This test is done to diagnose infections caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis or non-tuberculous bacteria in the central nervous system. It helps determine the appropriate treatment and prevent complications associated with these infections.

faqs.question: When is AFB-DNA (TB-PCR) Detection by Real Time PCR – CSF recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test is recommended for individuals who have symptoms such as severe headache, neck stiffness, confusion, or altered mental status, which could indicate an infection in the central nervous system. It is also useful for patients with a known or suspected diagnosis of tuberculosis meningitis or other central nervous system infections.

faqs.question: What if the results of AFB-DNA (TB-PCR) Detection by Real Time PCR – CSF are abnormal?
faqs.answer: If the test results are abnormal, i.e., positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, it confirms the presence of an active tuberculosis infection in the central nervous system. Follow-up tests may be done to determine drug resistance patterns and guide appropriate treatment.

faqs.question: What to expect during AFB-DNA (TB-PCR) Detection by Real Time PCR – CSF?
faqs.answer: During the AFB-DNA (TB-PCR) test, a small amount of cerebrospinal fluid is collected using a sterile container. The sample is then sent to the laboratory for analysis. The test is painless and usually takes about 24 hours to provide results.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before AFB-DNA (TB-PCR) Detection by Real Time PCR – CSF?
faqs.answer: There are no specific preparations necessary before this test. However, it's important to provide accurate clinical history, including any recent antibiotic use or other relevant medical information, to aid in the interpretation of test results. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with AFB-DNA (TB-PCR) Detection by Real Time PCR – CSF?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside this test include drug susceptibility testing to determine the most effective antibiotics for treating the infection, as well as other laboratory tests to assess the overall function of the central nervous system.

faqs.question: What is AFB-DNA (TB-PCR) Detection by Real Time PCR – CSF also known as?
faqs.answer: Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA testing, tuberculosis PCR testing

faqs.question: What is tuberculosis meningitis?
faqs.answer: Tuberculosis meningitis is a severe form of tuberculosis that affects the meninges, which are protective membranes covering the brain and spinal cord. It can cause symptoms such as headache, fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status, and seizures. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial to prevent complications and improve outcomes.

name: Galactomannan, Aspergillus Antigen Test by EIA – BAL

faqs.question: What does the Galactomannan, Aspergillus Antigen Test by EIA – BAL Fluid measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects galactomannan antigen in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid.

faqs.question: Why is the Galactomannan, Aspergillus Antigen Test by EIA – BAL Fluid done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose Aspergillus infections, especially in individuals with weakened immune systems. • To monitor the effectiveness of treatment for Aspergillus infections. • To guide the duration of antifungal therapy. • To identify patients at risk for invasive fungal infections.

faqs.question: When is the Galactomannan, Aspergillus Antigen Test by EIA – BAL Fluid recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test may be recommended for: • Individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS or undergoing organ transplantation. • Patients with suspected or confirmed fungal infections, especially Aspergillus infections. • Those undergoing treatment for Aspergillus infections to monitor response.

faqs.question: What if the results of the Galactomannan, Aspergillus Antigen Test by EIA – BAL Fluid are abnormal?
faqs.answer: An abnormal result indicates the presence of Aspergillus infection or other conditions that affect galactomannan levels. Elevated levels of galactomannan may suggest an active Aspergillus infection. Abnormal results do not necessarily indicate cancer or any other serious condition.

faqs.question: What to expect during the Galactomannan, Aspergillus Antigen Test by EIA – BAL Fluid?
faqs.answer: During the test: • A sample of bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid will be collected using a sterile, leak-proof container. • The sample will be sent to the laboratory for testing. • The laboratory will use the enzyme immunoassay (EIA) method to measure galactomannan levels in the BAL fluid sample.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the Galactomannan, Aspergillus Antigen Test by EIA – BAL Fluid?
faqs.answer: To prepare for this test: • Discuss your clinical history and any prescribed medications with your doctor. • Follow any specific instructions given by your healthcare provider. • No dietary or fasting restrictions are typically required. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the Galactomannan, Aspergillus Antigen Test by EIA – BAL Fluid?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be recommended alongside the Galactomannan, Aspergillus Antigen Test by EIA – BAL Fluid include: • Fungal culture: This test is performed to isolate and identify the specific fungus responsible for the infection. • Imaging studies: Chest X-ray or CT scan may be done to evaluate the extent of lung involvement.

faqs.question: What is the Galactomannan, Aspergillus Antigen Test by EIA – BAL Fluid also known as?
faqs.answer: Galactomannan Test, Aspergillus Antigen Test

faqs.question: What is an Aspergillus infection?
faqs.answer: Aspergillus infection is a fungal infection caused by the Aspergillus fungus. It commonly affects the lungs but can also occur in other organs. In individuals with weakened immune systems, these infections can be severe or life-threatening.

name: Parvovirus B19 DNA Detection by Real-time PCR - EDTA Blood
NextGen Hereditary Cancer Gene Panel, EDTA Blood
HGV-RNA Detection by PCR in Plasma

faqs.question: What does HGV-RNA Detection by PCR in Plasma measure?
faqs.answer: This test detects Hepatitis G Virus (HGV) RNA in your plasma using a technique called PCR.

faqs.question: Why is HGV-RNA Detection by PCR in Plasma done?
faqs.answer: • To detect HGV RNA by PCR in plasma • To assess the efficacy of treatment for Hepatitis G • To detect co-infection with other hepatitis viruses • To monitor liver function

faqs.question: When is HGV-RNA Detection recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend this test if you have • symptoms of acute or chronic Hepatitis G infection, • history of Hepatitis G or other viral hepatitis infections, • elevated liver enzyme levels, or • risk factors for hepatitis infections such as HIV, shared drug needles or unprotected sex with an infected person.

faqs.question: What if the results of the HGV-RNA Detection are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Elevated levels may indicate active Hepatitis G infection, which can cause liver inflammation and damage if left untreated.

faqs.question: What to expect during the HGV-RNA Detection in Plasma?
faqs.answer: This is a simple blood test. A healthcare professional will collect 3 ml of your EDTA plasma in a sterile plain vacutainer. The sample will then be sent to the laboratory for testing.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the HGV-RNA Detection?
faqs.answer: Before the test, inform your doctor if you have taken any medications or have any known allergies or medical conditions. You do not need to fast or make any special preparations for this test. Also, inform your doctor if you have any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with HGV-RNA Detection?
faqs.answer: Hepatitis A, B, and C testing: to rule out the presence of other hepatitis viruses Liver function tests: to evaluate the overall health of your liver

faqs.question: What is the HGV-RNA Detection by PCR in Plasma also known as?
faqs.answer: Hepatitis G Virus RNA PCR Test

faqs.question: What is Hepatitis G?
faqs.answer: Hepatitis G is a viral infection that attacks the liver and causes inflammation. Most cases of Hepatitis G resolve on their own without treatment. However, some people may develop chronic Hepatitis G infections that can lead to liver damage over time.

faqs.question: What does the JAK2 Mutation Test detect?
faqs.answer: It detects the JAK2 V617F gene mutation associated with myeloproliferative neoplasms like Polycythaemia Vera, ET, and Myelofibrosis.

faqs.question: Who should get a JAK2 Mutation Test?
faqs.answer: Individuals with high blood counts, blood clots, or symptoms suggestive of a bone marrow disorder.

faqs.question: Is fasting required before the test?
faqs.answer: No, fasting is not required for this genetic test.

faqs.question: What does a positive JAK2 Mutation Test mean?
faqs.answer: It confirms the presence of the JAK2 mutation, supporting a diagnosis of an MPN.

faqs.question: What if my JAK2 test is negative but my blood counts are high?
faqs.answer: Your doctor may recommend further genetic tests like CALR, MPL, or JAK2 Exon 12.

faqs.question: How is the test performed?
faqs.answer: A simple blood draw followed by genetic analysis using Real-Time PCR.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get the report?
faqs.answer: Reports are available by 7:00 PM the next day after sample collection.

faqs.question: Can the test monitor treatment progress?
faqs.answer: Yes, it helps track disease status and response to targeted therapy.

faqs.question: Are there any risks to the test?
faqs.answer: Risks are minimal and limited to mild pain or bruising at the blood draw site.

name: AFB-Smear Examination by ZN Stain – Body Fluids

faqs.question: What does the AFB-Smear Examination by ZN Stain – Body Fluids measure?
faqs.answer: This test measures the presence of acid-fast bacilli (AFB) specific to Mycobacterium tuberculosis in different body fluids.

faqs.question: Why is the AFB-Smear Examination by ZN Stain – Body Fluids done?
faqs.answer: • To diagnose infection by tuberculosis • To monitor treatment effectiveness for tuberculosis • To identify other conditions caused by AFB bacteria • To assess the risk of developing tuberculosis

faqs.question: When is the AFB-Smear Examination by ZN Stain – Body Fluids recommended and who should take the test?
faqs.answer: This test may be recommended if • You have symptoms of tuberculosis, such as cough, weight loss, fever, and night sweats. • You have been exposed to someone with active tuberculosis. • Your doctor suspects other conditions caused by AFB bacteria. • You need to monitor the effectiveness of tuberculosis treatment.

faqs.question: What if the results of the AFB-Smear Examination by ZN Stain – Body Fluids are abnormal?
faqs.answer: Abnormal, i.e., positive results may suggest a tuberculosis infection or other conditions caused by AFB bacteria.

faqs.question: What to expect during the AFB-Smear Examination by ZN Stain – Body Fluids?
faqs.answer: • You will be required to provide a body fluid sample, such as pleural fluid, cerebrospinal fluid, or ascitic fluid. • The sample collection is a simple procedure and will be performed at the laboratory or a healthcare facility. • The sample will be stained using the Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) stain and examined under a microscope to detect the presence of acid-fast bacilli.

faqs.question: What preparations are required before the AFB-Smear Examination by ZN Stain – Body Fluids?
faqs.answer: Before the test: • Inform your doctor about any ongoing medications or medical conditions. • Ensure the specimen type, site, clinical history, and relevant information are properly mentioned on the test request form (TRF). • Follow any specific instructions provided by your doctor regarding fasting or other preparations. Please reach out to your healthcare provider for any specific requirements.

faqs.question: What other tests may be ordered with the AFB-Smear Examination by ZN Stain – Body Fluids?
faqs.answer: Other tests that may be ordered alongside AFB-Smear examination by ZN Stain for body fluids include: • Culture and Sensitivity testing to identify the specific type of bacteria causing infection and determine antibiotic susceptibility. • PCR tests to detect the genetic material of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, providing faster and more accurate results. • Chest X-ray or CT scan to evaluate lung involvement in tuberculosis cases.

faqs.question: What is the AFB-Smear Examination by ZN Stain – Body Fluids also known as?
faqs.answer: Acid-Fast Bacillus Smear Examination by Ziehl-Neelsen Stain for body fluids

faqs.question: What is tuberculosis?
faqs.answer: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacteria. It primarily affects the lungs but can also affect other parts of the body. Symptoms include persistent cough, weight loss, fever, night sweats, and fatigue.
